AI is both the best and worst thing to ever happen to mathematics

New Scientist September 11, 2026

Our best equations for describing the way fluids move were first written down 200 years ago. Ever since, we have been unable to answer a simple question about them: do they sometimes blow up? This explosive phrase has a precise mathematical meaning describing a situation where, apparently out of nowhere, part of the fluid starts to move infinitely fast. It would be like an infinite whirlpool forming in your bathtub in response to a flick of your toes.

Understanding the Navier-Stokes equations – named after the pair who discovered them – has been a long-running quest for mathematicians. So much so that the blow-up question sits on the list of prestigious Millennium Prize Problems, each of which comes with a $1 million reward for solving.

This week, OpenAI stunned the world of mathematics with its announcement that its AI agents have finally found the answer: the equations do sometimes blow up. The implication isn’t that fluids will start misbehaving, but instead that the equations aren’t perfect. This is good news for your bathtub. Mathematics, however, may never be the same again.

Advertisement

Terence Tao: AI companies are harming mathematics

The reason for this isn’t the result itself. The Navier-Stokes equations have already proven themselves to be incredibly useful many times over, in applications ranging from making better airplane wings to modelling the flow of fluids through artificial hearts. Mathematicians had a suspicion that blow-ups were possible; now they know for sure.

That isn’t to underplay the discovery – it is one of the biggest mathematical breakthroughs in decades. But the way it has happened, and the resulting fallout, is what will have the most dramatic effect on mathematics for years to come.

OpenAI began working on the problem after it got wind that a pair of mathematicians had made some progress on it, which hadn’t yet been published. Researchers at the tech company decided to set thousands of AI agents on solving the problem. Just 88 hours later, they were done.

OpenAI has solved the Navier-Stokes Millennium problem using $15m of AI effort

Over the past few months, AI has made breakthrough after breakthrough in mathematics, with this most recent development being by far the most impressive. It wasn’t that long ago that mathematics was a bit of an embarrassment for AI because it was so bad at it; now it is shockingly good. How many other long-standing mathematical conundrums will fall to AI is uncertain, but it will surely be many. OpenAI has already said it has made “substantial progress” on another of the Millennium Prize Problems.

But AI proofs aren’t a straight replacement for human ones. Mathematicians want to know the why; AIs not so much.

The great mathematician Paul Erdős believed that mathematical truth exists independently of humanity in a sort of celestial book, and it is the job of mathematicians to discover what is in it. Sometimes, a mathematician would discover a logical argument that was so insightful and so elegant that it would bring a fresh understanding or a completely new way of thinking. Erdős would declare that a proof like this was “straight from The Book”. It’s fair to say that OpenAI’s effort wouldn’t make the cut.

That is because AIs tend to produce hard-to-follow, convoluted arguments. For the sake of proving a theorem, this doesn’t really matter, thanks to the magic of a process called formalisation, where proofs can be turned into code that can be rigorously checked by computers. But for the sake of gaining insight, it is lacking.

Subscriber-only newsletter

So, where does this leave mathematics? Clearly, the AI mathematical revolution has arrived. It is a new era where we will have many more answers than explanations, and unpicking it all won’t be easy. It isn’t just the Navier-Stokes equations that AI has blown up, but mathematics itself.

These are unprecedented times, and yet mathematics has gone through upheaval before. When René Descartes made the link between geometry and algebra in the 17th century, showing that shapes could be written as equations, he completely transformed the toolkit available to mathematicians.

Geometry, however, had been the darling of mathematics since the ancient Greeks. It was trusted and considered pure. Mathematicians worried that the job would make them drones who simply manipulated symbols and came up with no new insights. Philosopher Thomas Hobbes described the approach as a “scab of symbols”.

But 300 years later, it is indisputable that making this link between algebra and geometry was a good thing. Without it, there would be no calculus or relativity – in fact, modern science would be completely unrecognisable. Perhaps AI will have a similar effect.

Mathematicians now have an imperfect truth machine that spits out mathematical answers. There are big challenges ahead regarding how to use it, who gets access and what role AI companies should play, but it is a tool that has the potential to allow mathematicians to make progress much faster than before. AI may end up being the best and worst thing to have ever happened to mathematics.

Southland slink skin operator protests at council with animal carcasses

New Zealand Herald September 14, 2026

Eddie Zhi's business NZAgri Development Ltd processes the skins of dead lambs and calves, and has hit legal speed bumps. Photo / Michael Craig

A disgruntled slink skin operator who arrived at Invercargill council buildings with dead animals could be trespassed.

Da Cheng “Eddie” Zhi visited two council offices on Friday to protest after receiving enforcement orders the week before.

His business NZAgri Development Ltd processes the skins of dead lambs and calves at a factory south of Gore, but has hit legal speed bumps.

Environment Southland announced last week that the Environment Court had granted the regional council interim enforcement orders imposing restrictions on Zhi and his company, including cessation of processing and removal of carcasses.

The orders were not well received by Zhi, who emailed about 100 people early on Friday about his intention to protest, with “many trucks and utes, pregnant women and old people, under educated desperate workers in proverty [sic]”.

A follow-up message mid-morning Friday provided arrival times at Environment Southland and Southland District Council, with recipients for both emails including council representatives, lawyers, members of Parliament and media.

Zhi’s behaviour at Environment Southland led to a letter from the council’s lawyer informing him the local authority intends to trespass him.

“While we understand that protesters conducted themselves in a peaceful and orderly manner, we understand there were instances where you acted in an aggressive or threatening manner towards those present at Council’s premises,” the letter said.

“In particular, we understand your behaviour was sufficiently aggressive or threatening at one point that it prompted police to be called.”

The letter said although Zhi was advised not to enter the building due to previous behaviour which had led to all communication needing to go through the lawyer, it was understood he came back in the afternoon and “presented in an agitated state towards Council staff”.

“We also understand that you intend to return to the Council’s premises next Monday to conduct another protest, with weekly protests after that,” the letter said.

On Sunday night, Zhi rejected allegations of acting aggressively or threateningly during the protest.

He said three police officers attended for about half an hour, but both parties were on good terms with the officers.

“At no time was the protest anything other than peaceful,” Zhi said.

“We are passionate about defending our rights, our business and the livelihoods of our workers, but we remained respectful toward the police, Council staff and everyone else present.”

Zhi opposed the notice and said the protest would escalate on Monday unless Environment Southland acknowledged it had received the written request and responded constructively.

On Monday, Zhi told Local Democracy Reporting three “intimidating” security guards had barred entry to Environment Southland during Friday’s protest.

Zhi is the sole director of NZAgri Development Ltd, registered in July 2024.

Environment Southland said last week he was facing seven charges relating to operations at the factory between August 1 and September 26, 2025.

Six charges related to the discharge of blood, leachate or contaminants to land which could enter water, and the seventh was for failing to comply with an abatement notice.

Asked to confirm the trespass letter, Environment Southland said it would “take the necessary steps, which may include issuing a trespass notice” if a demonstration raised concerns.

Southland District Council had also laid charges, the regional council said.

Bequest of Ron Gillatt gifts unprecedented $60m to Christchurch charities

New Zealand Herald September 14, 2026

Ron Gillatt and his wife Joan left a $60m fortune to 15 Christchurch charities and clubs. Photo / Anna Heath (NZME), The Ron & Joan Gillatt Charitable Trust

Ron Gillatt died in Christchurch in early 2024, aged 83. The former BNZ manager loved trains and trams and cats. He seemed to have been a hoarder and left behind a modest house stuffed with junk and infested with silverfish – along with a well-managed pile of cash, shares and bonds worth more than $60 million.

A registered charity set up after his death, in accordance with his and his late wife’s precise instructions, appears to be the largest charitable bequest in South Island history.

The Ron and Joan Gillatt Charitable Trust has begun to distribute millions in annual funding for 15 largely Christchurch-based clubs, societies and charities, with distributions designed to continue into perpetuity.

Kathy Gillatt, whose husband is Ron’s cousin, said Ron and Joan – the couple had been married for many decades until her death in 2021 – lived a very private life, and this continued to their deaths. She said Ron wanted a private funeral, and his death was only announced publicly afterwards in a brief notice in the Press.

Kathy said Ron long had an interest in equity investing – “Mainly it was shares, the sharemarket. He was the king of the sharemarket,” she said – and he was an enthusiastic disciple of value investor and Nebraska-based billionaire, Warren Buffett.

“We buried him with his latest Warren Buffett book,” she said of Gillatt’s 2024 funeral.

The Companies Office records Gillatt remained an active investor until the first decade of the 2000s, and had bought stakes in dozens of startups. At one stage he was a 7% shareholder in Syft Technologies.

“They were both very special people, but very modest and unassuming,” Kathy said.

The Gillatts’ Avonhead home was sold by estate executors last year for $970,000.

“He caught the bus, using his [Super Gold] card so that was free, so he and they lived a very quiet and unassuming life. He was a banker with the BNZ, a bank manager,” she said.

He had kept a very low profile during his life. Newspaper archives record him receiving prizes for banking and securities studies while at Canterbury University in the 1960s, but he was quoted just once in news media during his lifetime.

In 1994, at the 25th anniversary of Tait Electronics, Gillatt spoke in honour of founder Sir Angus Tait. “In my opinion he is a great man ... though he is self-effacing and always gives credit to others,” the Press reported Gillatt saying.

Gillatt had managed the BNZ’s relationship with Tait since the technology company’s formation, and retired in 1993 as the bank’s business manager.

Ron and Joan had given considerable thought to what should happen to their discreet fortune after their passing, with the Ron and Joan Gillatt Charitable Trust founded in 2001.

Wynn Williams partner Annabel Sheppard assisted the Gillatts with the trust’s formation 25 years ago, and became a trustee after Ron’s death in order to manage his extraordinary bequest.

Sheppard told the Herald it was a privilege to have known the couple.

“They were both only children, Ron and Joan, and they didn’t have children, and they were philanthropic, and they have set up a legacy forever,” she said.

The trust’s first set of financial accounts, to March 2025, show it held $9m in cash, $37.9m in shares and another $13.5m in bonds for a total capital base of $60.4m.

The trust is structured to be perpetual, and its deed calls for two-thirds of surpluses to be reinvested, and the remaining third divided up in a precise formula to be annually distributed to 15 Christchurch-based charities, churches and clubs to help fund capital expenditure.

With this setup, presuming relatively conservative 6% returns, trust capital is likely to grow beyond $100m by the end of the next decade and provide an ever-rising stream of funding for its beneficiaries.

Beneficiaries spoken to by the Herald this week said the first distribution was made late last year, but they had been informed that one-off costs incurred on establishment – and capital growth – would likely see larger distributions in future.

One quarter of trust distributions – effectively the proceeds of $15m in capital – are flagged for the tram and model railway enthusiasts based at Ferrymead Heritage Park.

One fifth of distributions (20%) – the largest individual beneficiary share – is directed to flow to the Tramway Historical Society (THS). Another twentieth (5%) is going to the modest Garden City Model Railway Club.

The bequest provides outsized financial backing for the two organisations. THS recorded $71,762 of income last year, and the Model Railway Club recorded just $46,812. Both groups were unaware of Gillatt’s intentions – or in the latter case, even his existence – before being contacted by the Trust.

Ron Gillatt had been a member of THS since 2010, treasurer and former president Stephen Taylor said.

Gillatt was said not to have been particularly interested in driving or working on trams, but he and his wife were regular attendees at society social functions.

Taylor said a decade ago, THS was struggling to fundraise $100,000 for a storage building to keep historic and work-in-progress machinery out of the weather.

“He brought out a chequebook – back in the days when there were chequebooks – and was sort of willing to write us a cheque on the spot, so long as we agreed to pay him back in the fullness of time,” Taylor said.

THS ultimately declined the loan offer, worried about the effect of a liability on its cash-strapped balance sheet, and eventually raised the funds piecemeal in the following years.

Gillatt’s last involvement at THS was attending its AGM in September 2023, a few months before his death.

“At that stage Joan had passed. Ron didn’t drive, so he relied on Joan to get to meetings, and after she passed he would take the bus,” Taylor said. “That was the last time we’d seen him.”

It was only after his death, as lawyers sought to settle paperwork, that Taylor became aware THS was listed as the primary beneficiary of Gillatt’s extraordinarily large bequest.

“We think on a large scale, but unfortunately our finances weren’t able to support that,” Taylor said.

Things have now changed: “A lot of projects that were potentially going to happen [over] a long period of time can be done sooner and quicker.”

Douglas Mack, the president of the Model Railway Club, said he was unaware Gillatt even existed until contacted by the trust last year – more than a year after Ron’s passing – and they could only speculate how they had been named beneficiaries.

“I think he had some involvement with the THS at Ferrymead. But it appears that he just maybe went for a walk around the park and he found us and happened to talk to one of our members and he was impressed with what we were doing,” he said.

Remaining beneficiaries were a mixture of healthcare providers and local churches, schools and institutions that featured in Ron and Joan’s life.

The Fred Hollows Foundation and the Christchurch Charity Hospital are each directed to receive 10% of proceeds. The Order of St John South Island Region Trust Board and the Christchurch branch of the Nurse Maude District Nursing Association are each to receive 5%.

Hagley Community College and Riccarton High School – attended by Ron and Joan as children – are each to receive 5% to provide scholarships for students to attend university. Two Anglican churches in Halswell and Hornby, and the Halswell Community Hall, are also flagged as 5% beneficiaries.

Rhema Media and the Cats Protection League Canterbury, each getting a 5% share, round out the list of recipients.

The latter beneficiary was subject to a 2021 amendment to trust rules requiring the League to “supervise the ongoing welfare of any cats that are owned by Ronald Joseph Gillatt at the date of his death”.

This provision was ultimately not required: “Sadly the Gillatt’s cat died before they did,” Sheppard told the Herald.

Sheppard’s role with the trust has not just been bearing good news to beneficiaries. In the months after Ron’s passing, she had to go to the High Court at Christchurch to vary the terms of the trust after finding her settlor’s collecting of physical artefacts did not match his financial management.

The court heard the trust had originally been instructed to preserve and protect his beloved collection of stamps, DVDs and magazines, and ensure his 73-piece art collection found a good home – ideally public display at the Christchurch Art Gallery.

Sheppard submitted that what she found at Gillatt’s home had little value, or worse. Much of it was “rubbish with no enduring importance”.

Justice Rachel Dunningham records: “She was shocked at the sheer amount of property stored there. Furthermore, it was haphazardly stored, some of it was infested with silverfish and insects, and much of it was valueless paperwork.”

The stamp collection was valued in its entirety as possibly being worth $3000, but a valuer said it was “not readily marketable”. The artworks ranged in value from $20 to $1600 each, but experts said none were considered significant enough to display in any New Zealand public collection.

Sheppard submitted that being required to indefinitely preserve items of dubious or no value would not serve a charitable purpose and would be a drain on trust resources.

Justice Dunningham granted the orders, and directed the chattels be disposed of as trustees deemed fit.

The Gillatt’s bequest is believed to be the third-largest charitable donation in New Zealand history, behind only US billionaire Julian Robertson’s bequest of $200m worth of paintings to the Auckland Art Gallery in 2022 and Auckland farmer Harold Plumley’s gift of $122m to the Auckland Catholic Church after his death in 2016.

Matt Nippert is an Auckland-based investigations reporter covering the intersection of politics and business. He has won more than a dozen awards for his journalism – including twice being named Reporter of the Year – and joined the Herald in 2014 after having spent the decade prior reporting from business newspapers and national magazines.

Quick change to fast-track law being pushed through Parliament this week

New Zealand Herald September 14, 2026

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

This is a modal window.

Beginning of dialog window. Escape will cancel and close the window.

End of dialog window.

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

Changes to laws that will affect fast-track developments are being welcomed by councils, but they are pushing for the government to do more.

MPs will this week vote on an amendment to local government laws that’ll allow councils to claw back some of the costs of infrastructure from fast-track developers.

As revealed by the Herald last month, Infrastructure Minister Chris Bishop has reacted to the outrage over some residential fast-track developments by making tweaks to the fees developers pay to councils, known as development contributions.

While it won’t apply to those already approved such as Delmore and Sunfield in Auckland and Homestead Bay in Queenstown, it will impact those in other stages of the fast-track system.

The amendment to a Local Government Bill will “ensure councils can set appropriate development contributions that reflect the growth-related infrastructure costs associated with fast-track projects”, Bishop said.

“In response to out of sequence growth, mainly housing projects, councils will be able to amend their development contributions.

“It’s a complicated area of policy, at the moment the charges are locked in at the time a consent is granted and sometimes it can end up out of whack with what it should be.”

He said in most cases, it will mean developers paying more to councils.

It will be law by Thursday, he expected.

“Where a development creates additional infrastructure costs, an appropriate share should be met by the development rather than being shifted onto existing ratepayers,” Bishop said.

“It was a pragmatic response to something that needed fixing.”

He’s met with a lot of the mayors who have been concerned and made it clear to him they are worried about the looming costs.

Local Government New Zealand (LGNZ) has joined a chorus of mayors calling for residential developments to be paused.

LGNZ vice-president Dan Gordon welcomed Bishop’s move to make changes to development contributions.

“Today’s announcement shows the Government is listening,” Gordon said.

“We welcome the Government’s decision to include projects with a substantive application already lodged. This strengthening of development contributions was one of the recommendations in LGNZ’s four-point plan to ensure growth pays for growth and communities aren’t left carrying costs they didn’t create.”

“This is a positive step and an acknowledgment that improvements were needed to the way infrastructure costs are recovered under Fast-track. However, they’ll come too late for already approved projects, which means that councils still lose out on significant revenue.”

Auckland councillor Richard Hills, an outspoken critic of some of the developments, said he too was pleased the Government was listening.

“It’s too late and fixes one glaring error,” Hills told the Herald.

“That error has already locked in a $450-650m cost to all Auckland ratepayers and taxpayers which is the estimated amount we can’t now retrospectively recover through Development Contributions for Sunfield and Delmore.

“The change doesn’t allow us to recover the costs of maintaining and running services to these unplanned communities, we estimate those costs to be in the billions, not millions.”

Auckland Council last week voted to look at ways to either require developers to pay more for fast-track projects or send a message to residents that the council will not provide any services to them.

Hills said today’s move would not change the council’s position.

“We are considering all options to charge costs back to these developments and we are serious about finding ways to not provide these places with things like noise control, buses, animal control and other services.

“Fast track for residential developments is not how you plan a city, but it is how you shovel massive social, environmental and economic costs onto all Aucklanders and the next generation,” Hills said.

He’s urging all parties running for government to campaign on removing residential from fast track and stop taking the local out of local government.

LGNZ said there’s more work to do.

“We still think there’s merit in pausing future referrals, requiring consideration of cumulative effects, and reviewing Fast-track for housing to ensure it works well with the new planning system.

“We’d now like to see the remaining recommendations in our four-point plan progressed. We’d welcome working with Minister Bishop and Minister Watts to make Fast-track work on the ground,” Gordon said.

That four-point plan includes the temporary pause on ministerial referrals to the scheme, requiring the fast-track panel to consider the cumulative effects of multiple projects in one area and commission a longer-term review of the system to ensure it fits in with the new planning system developed by replacing the Resource Management Act.

LGNZs move follows letters sent by Auckland, Queenstown, Waimakariri and Selwyn councils demanding a pause on fast-track housing projects.

The law change will also allow councils to use development contributions to recover the capital costs incurred by another council in meeting the increased demands on their infrastructure attributable to growth imposed by fast-track development.

That portion of funds can then be transferred back to that council.

Local Government Minister Simon Watts says councils will be able to amend their development contribution policies where necessary to recover eligible growth-related costs.

“Importantly, councils will be able to make those targeted amendments without going through the usual consultation process, allowing them to respond quickly where an existing policy does not adequately reflect the infrastructure demands of a development,” Watts said.

“Any amendment will need to be adopted within six months of Fast-track approval, notified to the authorised person and published as soon as practicable.

“We are also addressing cross-boundary infrastructure costs. Where growth in one council area creates eligible infrastructure costs for another council, the collecting council will be able to recover those costs and transfer the appropriate share of the development contribution.”

The changes will apply to all projects, unless an applicant has received a draft decision to approve or decline a project.

“This creates a clear transition point and helps councils recover infrastructure costs from eligible projects while giving certainty to projects within the fast-track process,” Bishop said.

“Fast-track has been a much-needed circuit breaker for projects that should be creating jobs, delivering homes and growing local economies. These changes maintain that certainty and effectiveness while making sure the infrastructure funding system can keep up.”

A petition by residents of Waimauku West calling for a project there to be halted is also gaining support.

Katie Bradford is a Senior Correspondent at the Herald. She has been a broadcast journalist for over 20 years and was based in the press gallery for 10 years. She specialises in politics, business and Auckland issues.

Tauranga Hospital Emergency Department nurses declare state of emergency

New Zealand Herald September 14, 2026

Nurses at Tauranga Hospital Emergency Department have declared a state of emergency. Photo / Kelly O'Hara

Nurses at Tauranga Hospital have declared a state of emergency after a patient collapsed in the Emergency Department waiting room.

More than 100 New Zealand Nurses Organisation (NZNO) members and ED nursing staff wrote to Health New Zealand Te Whatu Ora’s chief executive and the Midland/Te Manawa Taki region’s executive director on September 8.

They called for urgent recruitment, saying “exceptional demand” has become their “daily reality”.

The chief executive acknowledged the department’s pressures and asked the executive director to meet with the union by September 22 to implement a plan that includes increased staffing.

It comes after a Tauranga Hospital ED doctor called for “double” the number of beds because patients were “in corridors 24/7”.

Health NZ said a “significantly larger” ED was planned for the hospital as part of a planned redevelopment.

The national spotlight has been on ED staffing after incidences of patient collapse and death in the Waikato Hospital ED.

NZNO delegate John Wylie said he could not recall any recent day when the Tauranga ED was not at more than 100% capacity.

“We are often working at more than 150% capacity …

“Ultimately, patients pay the price for hospitals that are continuously understaffed and under-resourced.”

Wylie said staff were assessing and treating some patients in corridors due to increasing capacity.

“Patients are at risk because of the increasing demand without the increase in staff to match this.

“Staff are stretched too thin and can’t give patients the care they need.”

The union’s letter said the ED was “operating over capacity every day”.

“What should be considered exceptional demand has become our daily reality.”

It said staff were being asked to manage increasing patient numbers with “inadequate resources”, the risks of which were “no longer theoretical”.

The letter said a patient collapsed in an ED waiting room toilet and was discovered by a member of the public, who alerted staff and triggered an emergency response.

While the circumstances would be reviewed, “it serves as a stark reminder of the risks created when overcrowding becomes normalised and departments are required to operate beyond their capacity every day”.

“We are increasingly concerned that without urgent action to address capacity and staffing pressures, further serious incidents and preventable harm will occur.”

Workforce modelling showed more nurses were needed “to safely meet patient demand and service requirements”, the letter said.

In the letter, staff called for Health NZ’s urgent approval to recruit 16.78 fulltime equivalent (FTE) nurses – a figure identified through the care capacity demand management (CCDM) process.

In a September 9 response to the union, Health NZ chief executive Dale Bramley said ensuring Tauranga ED had the workforce and resources it needed to provide safe, high-quality care was a priority.

“I acknowledge the sustained pressures experienced by the department and the impact these can have on both staff wellbeing and the delivery of patient care.”

Bramley said decisions about staffing establishments and workforce sat with Health NZ Midland executive regional director Cath Cronin and Bay of Plenty interim operations group director Jo Gibbs.

He asked them to meet with the union to discuss its concerns and to implement a plan that “includes an uplift to staffing numbers”.

Bramley said Health NZ was committed to working alongside staff to ensure workforce planning and service developments kept pace with the needs of the fast-growing Bay of Plenty community.

He said he valued the dedication and contributions of Tauranga ED staff.

In a statement to the Bay of Plenty Times last night, Cronin said she and Gibbs had offered to meet with Tauranga Hospital staff and were working out a suitable time.

She said Health NZ Bay of Plenty continued investing in workforce capacity and service improvements. Recruitment was under way for 6.0 FTE registered nurses, with 2.4 FTE starting their new positions shortly.

The agency also used casual staff and overtime to support service demand and unplanned leave, she said.

Cronin said workforce capacity and capability must evolve alongside demand as the community grew.

The considerations under way at local and national levels, including CCDM, would help inform future decisions about the support and investment required for Tauranga ED, she said.

“We are committed to ensuring the concerns raised by staff are part of those discussions.”

Cronin said a patient experienced a medical event while attending Tauranga Hospital’s ED on August 25. Staff responded immediately.

The patient was triaged on arrival, and the medical event occurred about two hours after they presented to the ED. The patient was successfully treated, Cronin said.

“We remain focused on ensuring people in Bay of Plenty continue to have access to timely emergency care and acknowledge the dedication of our staff, who continue to provide high-quality care under significant pressure.”

Court fight launched to free Manurewa dog Fat Boy from Auckland Council custody

New Zealand Herald September 14, 2026

Fat Boy was uplifted from Desiree Clarkson’s Manurewa address on August 18 and is being held at an Auckland Council animal shelter. Photo / Michael Craig

A legal fight has been launched to free Fat Boy after the accused cat-killing dog was seized by Auckland Council.

An application for an interim injunction has been filed after the American Staffordshire terrier cross Siberian Husky was uplifted from Desiree Clarkson’s Manurewa home on August 18.

An injunction hearing is set for October 29.

The seizure followed Clarkson being disqualified from owning dogs after she received nine infringement notices over two years.

Clarkson previously claimed animal management officers unfairly targeted her and spent extended periods waiting outside her home, allegations the council rejects.

Contact reporter Rachel Maher

A council spokesperson said they could not comment further while the matter was before the courts.

However, Auckland Council animal management manager Elly Waitoa confirmed Fat Boy was being held at a council animal shelter.

Because Clarkson has been disqualified from owning dogs, she is legally prevented from reclaiming Fat Boy or possessing, having custody of, or controlling any dog.

The council said the dog could only be claimed by a new owner if they could prove ownership had been transferred before the 14-day period after Clarkson’s disqualification and all outstanding fees had been paid.

Otherwise, Fat Boy would legally become council property once the required seven-day holding period had ended.

Fat Boy first came to the council’s attention in June 2024 after being found roaming while unregistered.

Further infringement notices followed after he was found roaming twice in early 2025 and again in August, when he was also unregistered.

In February 2025, Fat Boy was impounded after allegedly killing a pet cat. The attack could not be substantiated, but Clarkson was fined for allowing him to roam.

Three more roaming incidents were recorded in March 2026.

Fat Boy was again accused of killing a cat while roaming in May. That allegation could not be proven, but the council found sufficient evidence he had been roaming.

Fat Boy was later classified as a menacing dog and Clarkson received another infringement notice for failing to keep the animal under control.

By May this year, the council had issued Clarkson nine infringement notices over two years.

The council said the persistent offending, despite education and enforcement action, showed Clarkson had failed to meet the responsibilities of a dog owner and supported its recommendation to uphold her disqualification.

In a written objection, Clarkson claimed officers “harassed me and my dog by spending most of the time in a day sitting in our driveway parking area just waiting”.

She also alleged she had received infringement notices relating to dogs that did not belong to her, including one that had died “a long time ago”, and another neighbourhood dog that regularly visited her property.

Clarkson claimed an animal management officer responded “in a cheeky smart response” when she and her neighbours raised concerns about officers waiting in their shared driveway.

Acting animal management manager Nikki Cripps rejected Clarkson’s allegations that officers had targeted or harassed her.

Cripps said officers attended the property in response to public reports about roaming dogs and observed the dogs roaming during proactive patrols.

On several occasions, officers followed the dogs back to the property, she said.

“At no time were officers parked outside the property for extended periods.”

At a Regulatory and Safety Committee meeting in July, members heard Clarkson’s objection but decided to uphold their initial decision.

Clarkson will not be allowed to own dogs until December 2028.

Attempts to reach Clarkson last week were unsuccessful.

Rachel Maher is the education correspondent for the New Zealand Herald. She also covers other topics such as Auckland issues, crime and local government. She started at the Herald as a breaking news journalist in 2022, before joining the Auckland team this year.

Oranga Tamariki staff present during ‘walking the line’ assault

New Zealand Herald September 14, 2026

A young person was slapped and hit by other teenagers as he was discharged from Korowai Manaaki in March. Photo / RNZ, Peter de Graaf

By Lillian Hanly of RNZ

Oranga Tamariki has confirmed that staff were present during the assault of a young person by his peers in a ritual attack known as “walking the line”.

The Ministry for Children told RNZ the “action or inaction” in this case was being addressed and it could not provide further details about why staff did not stop the assault.

RNZ revealed last month that a young person had been slapped and hit by other teenagers as he was discharged from youth justice residence Korowai Manaaki in March.

Official Oranga Tamariki (OT) documents seen by RNZ confirmed that a “walking the line” assault took place.

That was explained as a situation where young people stand on either side of the internal door of the main entrance to the unit and wait to farewell the young person being discharged.

In this instance, three young people stood on one side and two on the other.

The document described the young person being discharged as standing at the top of the line. It said that: “he appeared nervous and was hesitant to walk towards the door”.

The incident was referred to police and an employment investigation had commenced.

RNZ requested further information about the assault and was told that at the time of the incident in question, “kaimahi were present in the unit with the rangatahi”.

OT also confirmed that police had closed their investigation with no charges made and no further action, advising OT there was “no evidence of criminal offending by either the rangatahi involved or the kaimahi”.

At the time of the request made to OT for further information in mid-August, OT said an employment process was still underway regarding the matter.

RNZ then asked why staff did not stop the assault from happening.

Oranga Tamariki Youth Justice Services and Residential Care deputy chief executive Dean Winter responded, saying “staff action or inaction in this case is being addressed appropriately and we cannot provide further details”.

“We have already taken steps with Korowai Manaaki kaimahi to reinforce expectations for incident reporting,” he said, adding that any harm to rangatahi or kaimahi in their residences was unacceptable.

Flu season hitting children’s hospitals hard, extra paediatricians called in

New Zealand Herald September 14, 2026

That was an 85% increase since the end of July in the number of children admitted with the most severe respiratory symptoms. Photo / RNZ

By Rowan Quinn of RNZ

Extra paediatricians are being drafted in and elective procedures are still being called off in the busiest flu season for Auckland’s children’s hospitals in years.

PHF Science figures showed there had been about 70 children with the most severe respiratory symptoms admitted each week for the past four weeks to Kidz First and Starship hospitals.

That was an 85% increase since the end of July and did not reflect the total number of children in hospital with respiratory symptoms, or emergency presentations.

South Auckland paediatrician Dame Teuila Percival said this winter had been the worst for years – and the busiest she could remember.

It had been all-hands-on-deck at KidzFirst.

“People do extra shifts, we have senior medical officers like myself and others who work in places like psychiatry coming in, helping out doing more time in the ED,” Dame Teuila said.

Children were being admitted with a wide range of symptoms including dehydration, confusion from fever, vomiting, diarrhoea, difficulty breathing, a bad cough and needing oxygen, she said.

Some were in intensive care – usually because they needed high levels of support with breathing, she said.

“They’re taken care of very well when they’re there but it’s very stressful for parents and families to see their children so unwell.”

RNZ understands that Starship also remained very busy, with elective procedures still regularly deferred because the space was needed for acutely unwell children.

Dame Teuila said many of the most ill children were Pasifika or Māori.

It was great that the flu vaccine had been made free for under-5s this month, but she would like to see it free for everyone next winter, she said.

Flu often made its way around a family, and more vaccination would help.

“It’s not uncommon that the whole family come to ED – and we see all the children and the mum and the dad and everybody’s sick,” she said.

Dame Teuila said there needed to be more resources for general practice to be able to help more people get in to see their doctors before they get more ill.

“I do think getting to primary care is a barrier for a lot of families particularly if you have got two, three, four kids all sick. It’s very hard to get in to see someone at the moment in a timely way,” she said.

“My colleagues in primary care work really hard. They’re just under the pump when I speak to them on the phone as we all are. They just need more people,” she said

RNZ asked Health NZ for figures for children in other main hospitals in New Zealand, but it said they needed to go through the Official Information Act process which could take several weeks.

PHF Science kept combined figures for the two dedicated children’s hospitals in Auckland, which is why they were readily available.

A spokesperson said the figures, up to September 6, were part of its severe acute respiratory surveillance which only covered some of the most ill children.

Other respiratory hospitalisations would not be included.

- RNZ

Taane Natana murder trial: Jury hears Facebook Live made after Ruatoki shooting

New Zealand Herald September 14, 2026

Taane Natana is on trial in the High Court at Rotorua for the murder of Tuterangi Moeke.

Shortly after a man was shot dead through a car window, Taane Natana was on Facebook Live saying: “I blasted them up with my big rifle”.

A jury must decide whether Natana, 35, murdered Tuterangi Moeke on December 10, 2023, near Ruatoki – a rural settlement in the Eastern Bay of Plenty.

Natana has pleaded not guilty to murder and an alternative charge of discharging a firearm with intent to cause grievous bodily harm.

His trial began yesterday in the High Court at Rotorua.

It’s the Crown’s case that Natana shot Moeke after he was ambushed in what was supposed to be “one outs”, or a fist fight, near a bridge at Ruatoki.

Instead, Natana’s car was shot at and shrapnel hit his face. The Crown said Natana then chased Moeke’s car and fired two shots through the back window.

In her opening address to the jury, Crown prosecutor Larissa Mulder played snippets of the Facebook Live video recovered by police.

In the video, Natana described what had happened. He made threats to the person who shot at him: “You’re gonna f***in’ die ... You’re dead”.

He also said: “Yeah and I might’ve hit someone ... F*** it would’ve been straight through their car too. I blasted them up too with my big rifle. F*** it was cutting the car up”.

In his brief opening to the jury, Natana’s lawyer Steven Lack said the jury could not be sure it was Natana who pulled the trigger.

He warned that social media was “littered with untruths” and suggested Natana was performing to an audience “goading him along”.

Mulder told the jury Natana and Moeke had arranged a fight after an earlier exchange on Facebook.

On the night of December 9, Natana spent time with a woman who was a friend of Moeke’s partner.

The partner had driven the woman to Natana. Early the next morning, the two women drove to Huntly.

Moeke’s partner had been staying with the friend to have time away from Moeke, Mulder said.

On the morning of December 10, the woman posted on Facebook that she and Moeke’s partner were going to church.

Natana replied with two laughing emojis. Moeke then commented “what’s funny you little h**o”.

Mulder said the men moved the conversation to Facebook Messenger and arranged “one outs” that night. The messages were deleted and never recovered by police.

Mulder said both groups arrived in cars and with guns.

Moeke fired two rounds from his shotgun at Natana’s vehicle, piercing the car body and shattering windows. Shrapnel hit Natana in the face.

Moeke’s Mazda left but stopped about 650m away, where Moeke threw his shotgun into a paddock, Mulder said.

The car sped towards Whakatāne, pursued by Natana in his Mitsubishi.

Natana’s Mitsubishi caught up to the Mazda at the Reid Rd and Ruatoki Valley Rd intersection.

Mulder said two shots were fired into the rear of the Mazda, where Moeke was a passenger.

The driver realised Moeke had been shot and sped towards his Whakatāne home before going to Whakatāne Hospital, where Moeke was pronounced dead at 9.47pm.

Mulder said Natana went to his Ruatoki home and before 10pm went live on Facebook.

“The Crown says Taane Natana’s words implicate him either as the shooter or as a party to the shooting. Together with the other evidence, it will make you sure that he was in the Mitsubishi Outlander and is criminally liable for the death of Tuterangi Moeke.”

Lack said Natana did not shoot Moeke or agree or plan with anyone else to shoot him.

He said Moeke had “ambushed” Natana by challenging him to a fist fight, then lying in wait with a shotgun and firing at least two rounds at the car.

“There is no firearm that conclusively links him to the shooting, no ammunition, no physical evidence at all which establishes he fired the firearm.”

He said there was a gap in the Crown’s evidence. He also cautioned the jury about the Facebook live video.

“Just one or two scrolls through a Facebook, TikTok or Instagram feed is likely to turn any number of deceptions, any number of exaggerations.”

He said the jury might later decide Natana was embarrassed on the Facebook live because he was caught off guard by Moeke.

“You might think he was performing to an audience who were goading him with the comments and the questions throughout the live video.”

The trial is before Justice Greg Blanchard and is expected to take three weeks.

Kelly Makiha is a senior journalist who has reported for the Rotorua Daily Post for more than 25 years, covering mainly police, court, human interest and social issues.

Calvert-Lewin shows the way as Leeds thrash limp Newcastle and rise to third

The Guardian Mon, 14 Sep 2026 21:07:08 GMT

Leeds United’s magnificent start to the Premier League season continued with a statement victory over an appalling Newcastle United to move the Whites up to third in the table and offer further evidence a European push may not be beyond them this season.

After one of the most eye-­catching performances of the season so far, Leeds humiliated Newcastle on a night where Matthias Jaissle was given a stern lesson about the challenges the Premier League can provide. Leeds bullied the visitors physically from start to finish and now sit inside the Champions League places with two wins and two draws from their first four games.

Daniel Farke’s side, led by the ­outstanding Dominic Calvert-Lewin, remain unbeaten. In stark contrast, Jaissle’s bright start at Newcastle was brought to a shuddering halt under the lights in West Yorkshire.

His side were outplayed and, as mentioned, outmuscled by Leeds and the demeanour of the German on the Elland Road touchline became more and more exasperated as this challenging evening evolved. This was their first defeat under Jaissle, do not forget. So it is perhaps important not to over-react too much in these moments; but the manner of the loss will sting for sure.

With a raucous backing from both sets of supporters generating a ­fantastic atmosphere under the Elland Road lights, it was Leeds who began brightly. The first real chance came the way of the hosts, as James Justin and Jayden Bogle combined superbly with only a smart reflex save from Lukas Hornicek preventing Bogle’s clever effort on the turn from going in.

But at the other end, Newcastle were finding space in behind Leeds’ backline. However, their rhythm was stunted by the withdrawal of Nico González, who had suffered a heavy blow to the head in the opening minutes and was taken off midway through the first half for a concussion substitution.

That helped Leeds regain momentum. Bogle was surprisingly Leeds’ most potent attacking threat as he again tested Hornicek from range and as half-time approached, you sensed it was the hosts who were more likely to open the scoring. That moment duly arrived shortly after the half-hour mark as Ao Tanaka’s effort was declared a Lewis Miley own goal.

And while there was an element of fortune about the opener, there was nothing lucky about Leeds’ second just two minutes later as Steur’s wayward pass inside his own half was picked up by Bogle. Again, the hosts took full advantage down the right with Justin’s pinpoint cross superbly headed by Dominic Calvert-Lewin which brushed over Bogle on its way into the net.

Suddenly, Leeds were in complete control and Newcastle were a mess. It could and perhaps should have been three when Calvert-Lewin produced a magnificent reflex after Hornicek had done well to deny Gabriel Gudmundsson following his marauding run into the visitors’ box.

It would then get even better in first half injury time. Calvert-Lewin was causing mayhem among the Newcastle backline and after he snuck in behind, this time he had the composure to step around Sven Botman and slide the ball under Hornicek to make it three. Matthias Jaissle appeared stunned on the touchline: and he was not the only one.

Newcastle inexplicably did not learn their lesson during the half-time break, either. They were fortunate not to go four behind when Botman was the latest to get caught in possession close to his own goal, with Anton Stach arguably guilty of not doing better as he chipped into the side netting.

But it was not long until Leeds finally did have their fourth goal. The visitors made a mess of an Ethan Ampadu long throw-in to give Noah Okafor enough time to drill a well-placed effort past Hornicek and into the bottom corner. Elland Road – three-quarters of it, at least – had come alive. This was now turning into a party, with the home support demanding a fifth.

That fifth ultimately never arrived but it did not dampen the atmosphere. Nor too did the late goal from substitute Bazoumana Touré which at least afforded the support from Newcastle a consolation – but the damage had long since been done by a Leeds side who continue to impress.

AI-linked stocks slide after tech bosses call for slowdown in ‘reckless’ development

The Guardian Mon, 14 Sep 2026 21:01:55 GMT

Donald Trump dismisses attempts to increase controls on artificial intelligence as ‘sick conspiracy’

AI-linked stocks tumbled on Monday after the bosses of Anthropic, OpenAI and SpaceX called for a slowdown in AI “reckless” development, citing fears the technology could soon run out of control.

Shares in the semiconductor designer Nvidia – the world’s most valuable company – were down 3.3% by market closing in New York City, while Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) slid 4% and Micron Technology and Sandisk shares slumped by 5%. The tech-heavy Nasdaq index fund was down 0.5% by the end of the day.

The sell-off came after the chief executive of Anthropic, Dario Amodei, appealed at the weekend for the AI industry to “slow down”.

However, Donald Trump dismissed calls to increase controls on AI as a “sick conspiracy”.

In a social media post on Monday, the president wrote: “The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the USA has that, in spades!”

The president added that his administration had “stopped AI ‘people’ from doing bad, or potentially bad, ‘things,’ like Dario (Anthropic!)”.

“There is a SICK conspiracy going on against AI and Data Centers, and the only one that is happy about it is China. WHOEVER WINS AI, WINS!”, he wrote.

Shares in SoftBank, a Japanese investor that is a big backer of OpenAI, slumped 13%, while the South Korean Kospi stock index, which relies heavily on chipmakers that supply AI companies, dropped by 3%.

Shares in the big global microchip supplier Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company dropped 1.2%.

In Europe, shares in the Dutch tech manufacturer ASML, Europe’s biggest company by value and an important supplier for the semiconductor industry, slumped by 6%.

There was, however, a rally in shares that have been threatened by the rise of AI, including the advertising group WPP, which rose by 5% in London, and the analytics business Relx, which was also up 5%. The latter had suffered a sharp fall earlier this year after Anthropic launched a suite of new data and automation tools.

Amodei has said that “building too fast is reckless”, warning that a swarm of AI agents could cause hundreds of billions of dollars of damage by “taking over the entire internet” in future.

His claims have been disputed by some experts, but on Monday investors began to price in a slowdown that would make it harder for the industry to pay for hundreds of billions of dollar in investments in AI infrastructure.

The OpenAI CEO, Sam Altman, the Google DeepMind chief, Demis Hassabis, and SpaceX boss, Elon Musk, all posted support for Amodei’s essay on slowing AI development, titled “We Must Pace the Frontier”.

Altman added that he would match Amodei’s commitment to embedding outside evaluators within his company to verify safety practices.

Fears continue to grow over the rapid pace and lack of regulation in AI development. On Monday, a cross-party group of UK MPs and peers identified a series of human rights risks posed by AI, arguing that no country in the world had laws sufficient to contain them.

Sign up to Business Today

after newsletter promotion

Meanwhile, China’s top intelligence official warned that the use of AI by adversaries could pose a risk to the country’s political and social security.

Chen Yixin wrote in a government outlet on Sunday that advanced US models such as Anthropic’s Mythos and OpenAI’s GPT-5.5-Cyber could pose serious risks to Beijing’s critical information ​infrastructure, and called for a comprehensive strengthening of AI security.

Despite such concern about the risks around AI, Jim Reid, of Deutsche Bank, said intense competition in the sector meant it was unlikely AI companies would stop investing so heavily in their technology.

“The competitive race between companies and countries remains intense, and it’s difficult to imagine firms voluntarily stepping back while rivals continue to push ahead.” he said. “It is hard to see China standing still.

“If leading executives are openly discussing the risks of increasingly powerful systems, it could be them trying to get across how transformative they believe the technology may become and help advertise the power of their product.

“Rather than signalling less spending, it could simply be that a greater share of AI investment is directed towards safety, monitoring and governance alongside the continued build-out of compute infrastructure.”

Amodei’s warning came before reports emerged that Anthropic is on track to be profitable this quarter.

The company told investors that its adjusted operating income would be positive for a second quarter in a row, according to the Financial Times, in a big milestone as it prepares to list on the US stock market this year.

OpenAI has also suggested it will also join the stock market, although Altman said over the weekend that the company would not go public in 2026 owing to safety concerns with the technology.

Forever Home review – Graham Norton’s corpse-in the-basement thriller absolutely stinks

The Guardian Mon, 14 Sep 2026 21:00:16 GMT

Norton’s best selling novel hits the small screen in a flurry of murder, bad gags and ex-soap stars in drab cardigans drinking fake coffees. What a total yawn

‘What in the name of the Virgin Mother is that terrible honk?” bellows Moira (Denise Welch) as she staggers disgustedly around her daughter Carol’s kitchen. “The smell!” she continues, cheeks ballooning in horror as Carol (Amy Nuttall) – who is, you suspect, familiar with such theatrics – busies herself with the teabags. “Carol?! The smell.”

Moira – a vision of motherly forbearance in cerise elastane – is not the only one alarmed by the mysterious stench emanating from 7 Stable Row, the Edwardian domicile in which six-part thriller Forever Home does the bulk of its thrilling. Carol’s unblinking partner, Robert (Douglas Henshall, far better than he needs to be), wonders if the smell might be something to do with the drains. Robert’s son Kaden (Lewis Cope) suspects foxes. And Carol? Carol is as narked with the funk as the rest of them.

That said, she thinks it’s probably best not to mention the fact that it’s all down to the corpse that’s currently defrosting in the faulty freezer she has just discovered in the cellar. Not just yet, anyway. Wouldn’t want to put anyone off their garibaldis. Particularly as said stiff appears to be Robert’s first wife, a “cow” who had, according to an increasingly shifty Robert, buggered off with his brother 20 years ago. Determined to prove to herself that Robert – who is in the early stages of dementia – is innocent, Carol soon finds herself in an investigational pea-souper, a tangled web of murder and blah in which long-buried secrets emerge from yawn and etcetera.

All clear? Grand. And so, with nose pinched and buttocks clenched, we bash on.

Based on the bestselling novel by Graham Norton, Forever Home is the latest emission from Channel 5’s Indistinguishable Domestic Thriller Processing Complex™, the shadowy facility responsible for such mechanically separated tubes of bunkum as Number One Fan, For Her Sins, The Fortune and no-me-neither classic of the genre, The Game.

You know the deal: murder, betrayal, ex-soap actors in drab cardigans nursing visibly empty coffee mugs while standing alone in fitted kitchens from B&Q’s These Lies Are Tearing Your Marriage Apart Babes® range. Here, however, the custom blend of banality and absurdity is served with an unexpected accompaniment: humour. This is represented by lines such as “She doesn’t know her Van Goghs from her Van Dammes!” and a winking string motif that pops up whenever Forever Home wants us to know it’s safe to come out from behind the sofa.

So here is Robert’s daughter Sally (Jenny Walser), a gullible leisure centre receptionist engaged in a saucy subplot with adulterous spanner Patrick (James Baxter). “We can get married in Las Vegas!” she swoons during one of their clandestine bums’n’tums workouts in the leisure centre’s store room. “Grumph,” replies Patrick, his faithless bum cheeks clacking like castanets.

The soundtrack continues to tee-hee when an increasingly desperate Sally decides to befriend Patrick’s sweetly clueless wife, and refuses to let up even when, later, she starts secretly pawing through her underwear drawer.

When Carol finally shares her cadaver-based discovery with Moira, it’s party time at the giggle factory. You can’t tell the police, shrieks Moira. There’ll be trophy hunters. “This place will become like a grisly house of horrors! Robert … AKA Fred West!”

Does this lighthearted approach to unhilarious subjects (eg dismemberment and stalking) work? It does not. Does it at least offer the odd moment of blackly comic respite from what would otherwise be an unremittingly bleak catalogue of domestic traumas? Again, no.

Instead, we have a drama that crashes between tones and issues like a drunken soap, but without the earnestness or depth of characterisation that can make these things bearable. The only topic Forever Home considers a lol-free zone is Robert’s dementia. We know this because his scenes are accompanied by a sad piano rather than thigh-slapping and titters.

Nobody turns up to a weeknight Channel 5 thriller expecting prestige subtlety or searing psychological insight. But is it too much to ask for a script that doesn’t honk like a defrosting corpse? Suffice to say: don’t go into the cellar.

Forever Home is on Channel 5 now

New special envoy for Britons detained overseas warns of limits of role

The Guardian Mon, 14 Sep 2026 20:57:21 GMT

Alistair Burt speaks candidly about difficulties of tackling complex cases as families express concern over mandate

The special envoy for British citizens detained overseas has spoken about the difficulties he faces in his new role, as families express concern over the position’s mandate in complex consular cases.

In his first public engagement, Alistair Burt, the former Conservative Middle East minister, spoke candidly about the difficulties and limitations of the new appointment, made following years of mounting criticism of how the Foreign Office handled the cases of British citizens detained overseas.

“I don’t make policy. I’m not a minister. I don’t have that authority. It will ultimately be the foreign secretary and the prime minister who will need to make the changes in policy or changes in approach if required,” Burt told an audience in Westminster, following his appointment on Monday evening.

“The best thing I can do is not disguise from you the difficulties of the role,” added the former minister.

Burt, who plans to meet the new foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, later this week, was tipped for the post more than a year ago. Burt was candid about the complexities of detention cases and of his role to “kick the tyres” of the policies involved.

Burt, whose new role is appointed by the Foreign Office but not paid for by it, said he has already started to meet families of those with complex cases, and said there was “much to be gained” from stronger international condemnation.

There is a strong view that the US special presidential envoy for hostages has secured more success and clout inside the diplomatic system, and used more innovative techniques to negotiate the release of Americans.

Burt said he plans to meet his US and Canadian counterparts in the coming weeks, and is open to discussing broader cooperation with European leaders.

The Foreign Office describes the purpose of the role as being to advance the government’s commitment to British nationals in the “most difficult and complex detention cases overseas” at the direction of the foreign secretary. The role is intended to advocate within and represent government, and engage with families.

Speaking alongside Burt at Monday’s parliamentary event was Nazanin Zaghari-Ratcliffe, a dual national who was arbitrarily detained in Iran for six years before being released in 2022.

A documentary was played showing the ordeal her family went through to secure her release, as well as that of Anoosheh Ashoori, for whom a historic £400m debt was paid to Iran.

“I recognised the payment of the debt and I let my foreign secretary know repeatedly,” said Burt of Nazanin’s case, adding, “I got that one right.” That wasn’t the case, he admitted, for Matthew Hedges, a British academic sitting beside him, who was accused of spying for the UK government in the United Arab Emirates and was arrested and tortured.

“Other cases I didn’t handle as well as I would have liked,” said Burt. “I’m very grateful that Matthew has seen me since to talk about his experiences.”

While welcoming the appointment, Zaghari-Ratcliffe also expressed a fear of quiet diplomacy turning into an “excuse” for government inaction.

Lawyers and campaigners at the event also expressed concerns over the limited mandate of the special envoy role, and called for the position to be independent of the Foreign Office and for the UK to be bolder in its diplomacy.

In attendance was also Laila Soueif, who went on hunger strike in pursuit of freedom for her son, British-Egyptian activist Alaa Abd el-Fattah, who was released from an Egyptian jail in 2025 after serving six years, as well as Naomi Connell, a friend of Lindsay Foreman and Craig Foreman, who has campaigned for the couple’s release from Iran’s Evin prison.

Also present was Heather Cornelius, whose husband, Ryan, has been arbitrarily imprisoned in Dubai for more than 18 years. The family discussed their case with Burt when he was a minister in 2018, said Heather, expressing scepticism over whether the envoy role, which runs for 18 months, will do anything other than liaise with and reassure families.

“He’s not going in there saying: ‘Yes, I know I can make a difference, I know I can help these people.’ He’s not saying that. He’s just saying: ‘Well, it’s very difficult,’” said Cornelius, who delivered a letter to Andy Burnham earlier on Monday, asking for the prime minister to help secure her husband’s release.

“They’re relying on other countries being involved, and of course that’s good, but Britain can do something, and they can do more,” she added.

Ministers seek law change to make £72m donations to Reform illegal

The Guardian Mon, 14 Sep 2026 20:01:23 GMT

Andy Burnham’s government could thwart Reform’s unprecedented £72m donations with retrospective restrictions on political donors that will include tough new residency requirements, ministers have announced.

In a move that is likely to set off furious complaints from Nigel Farage’s party, the government will table amendments to legislation going through the House of Lords within weeks that puts the legality of Reform’s latest donations in doubt.

Senior Labour and union figures had urged ministers to look again at party funding rules after Reform announced at the weekend that two cryptocurrency billionaires, Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne, who have both previously been based overseas, were each donating £36m to the party.

Government sources, however, said the plans to strengthen the representation of the people bill had been under way for weeks, after MPs pushed for further action on domestic donations in the House of Commons.

Under the proposals, which are expected to be tabled at the Lords committee stage of the legislation, individual donors will have to prove their ongoing physical presence in the UK, in line with the residence requirements applied to other areas of government policy, such as tax status.

The extraordinary measure will be seen as a sign of the stakes attached to the donations, which would give Reform a vast advantage in organising supporters on the ground before the next election.

However, Farage acknowledged on Monday that Reform could fall foul of government moves to clamp down on foreign donors, although the party has said the £72m donations are in line with both current rules and those already voted on by MPs in the bill.

The legislation currently restricts donations from expats to £100,000, which would also apply for the first 12 months after they return to the UK – backdated to 25 March this year.

Ministers have already brought in a minimum residency requirement of the remainder of the calendar year in which they return, plus a further full year, meaning Reform may not be able to accept the £72m donations until January 2028.

Delo has been based in Hong Kong but said in April he would return to the UK to avoid restrictions, while Harborne was based in Thailand but is believed to have registered to vote in Hampshire in June.

“Both these donations are 100% compliant with the law today, of that there is no question whatsoever,” Farage told the BBC. When asked if the two billionaires were UK residents as of 25 March, he replied: “All I’m going to say is, with the law of the land as it stands, they are both compliant.”

Sharon Taylor, a Labour minister in the Lords, told peers that as well as donors having to demonstrate a “genuine and ongoing connection to the UK”, the government was also looking at further restrictions.

“We are considering how we will strengthen the residency requirements, including ensuring the length of time spent in the UK aligns with broader government policy,” Lady Taylor added.

However, MPs and peers who have been pushing for a full domestic donations cap are unlikely to be satisfied by the new amendments. Government sources have said they do not want to delay the bill’s progress further by considering such a cap, but are open-minded on further legislation. MPs have voiced anger in internal WhatsApp groups that the chance has been missed to cap domestic donations in this bill while it was in the Commons.

Angela Rayner, speaking at the TUC, criticised Reform for suggesting its donations from cryptocurrency billionaires were equivalent to the contributions from trade union members to Labour.

“How dare they try to compare money from a couple of crypto billionaires to union members’ subs? The most highly regulated political funding we can have,” the communities secretary said.

“It couldn’t be more different from a couple of offshore billionaires trying to buy our democracy … We will never undermine the rights of working people to organise collectively and democratically.”

Trade unions are set to issue a statement on Tuesday on political donations condemning attempts by Farage to compare wealthy individual donors with individual members who donate to Labour through their union, and urging the government to go further on political donations.

The head of Britain’s union movement, Paul Nowak, said the government must act to “stop the super-rich corrupting our politics”. But union sources had said there were “significant differences” between general secretaries on how to proceed.

Unite’s general secretary, Sharon Graham, on Sunday broke ranks and backed a limit on individual domestic donations. But others, including GMB chief Gary Smith, fear it would lead a future rightwing government to curb union donations.

Government sources said that calls from opposition parties for any changes to domestic donations to apply to the unions too were “not under active consideration”.

However, the government is understood to be looking at spending limits for parties, which are currently restricted to the year before a general election, with tighter limits in the weeks running up to polling day.

In a letter to the Electoral Commission in August, Rayner and Louise Haigh, the first secretary of state, wrote: “We believe spending limits on parties and candidates are too high, and ought to be reduced.”

The government has also set up a cross-government “task and finish” team to consider threats to UK democracy, including political finance, illegitimate influence, and broader threats to political equality.

Philip Rycroft, who produced an independent report on tightening electoral law around overseas donations, said the Reform donations reopened broader questions about donations and spending caps.

“The time has come when this does need a hard look. It would have been better if the government had started out before we had these huge donations coming down the track,” he said.

“But we have to ask the question, is this healthy for our democratic process to have more money coming from fewer people in bigger lumps?”

MPs who have campaigned for a donations cap are working with peers on a number of amendments to the bill which would tighten it up without having to wait for another act of parliament.

They include one to enable ministers to set a cap on all donations at a later date, and another to prevent spending limits being raised without Electoral Commission approval.

Teresa O’Neill, a shadow local government minister in the Lords, said some of the measures in the bill were deeply troubling. “Even just the perception of partisan, targeted legislation risks breaking down longstanding political conventions and, crucially, trust in the system,” she said.

Reform denounced the government’s existing plans, with Zia Yusuf, the party’s home affairs spokesperson, describing them on X as “an unprecedented step from a leftwing government to plunge Britain into dictatorship and communism”.

From influencers to brutal finishes, US Open 2026 was worst grand slam in recent memory

The Guardian Mon, 14 Sep 2026 19:48:31 GMT

Despite the drama on the court, the poor condition of Arthur Ashe Stadium was just one problem among many

At the end of another comically late night and early morning in Flushing Meadows, when the remaining spectators were departing, a familiar scene was unfolding on the US Open tournament grounds. A handful of workers had congregated directly beneath a hole in the ceiling inside one of the tournament shops as they tried to stop water from flowing out of a broken pipe and ruining thousands of pounds worth of merchandise below.

This was not a surprising sight. Upon entering Arthur Ashe Stadium this year, fans were greeted by some ominous signs: “Pardon our appearance while we write the next chapter of Arthur Ashe Stadium.” The tournament’s appearance, it must be said, was hideous. Inside the corridors and rooms at one of the biggest sporting events in the world, it felt like its main building was falling apart.

Seemingly every other day a new leak revealed itself in the media centre, with long plastic sheets attached from the ceiling to buckets on the floor containing the splashing in various parts of the room. In the nearby workers’ restaurant, a dramatic burst of water from the ceiling caused its closure for one day. Throughout the tournament, a colleague joked that most sane human beings would not return every day to work underneath a ceiling that seemed ready to collapse at any time. Elsewhere, numerous photographers reported feeling sick after inhaling fetid fumes from the drains in the photo pit.

This was the worst grand slam tournament in recent memory for various reasons. When people look back, 2026 will be remembered as the US Open’s year of the influencers, a group united by their talent for making everything about them. It takes a special level of foolishness to bring ring lights to a tennis match, loudly film TikTok videos in the middle of games and repeatedly stand up to take selfies during points. There is a widespread belief that everyone involved in the sport should help to “grow the game” at all costs. Sometimes, though, gatekeeping is great. Meanwhile, the general conversation on Ashe was so loud at times that even Aryna Sabalenka’s screams were drowned out.

Although the 16 hours of tennis between 11.30am on Tuesday and 3.33am on Wednesday provided one of the most spectacular quarter-final days in recent history, with four dramatic final sets in four matches, it is an obvious sign of dysfunction in this sport that tournament organisers still have not prioritised finding a real solution to these early morning finishes.

In the heat of battle, though, there was still so much to enjoy. Women’s tennis stole the show again as the entire top six reached the quarter-finals and, for the first time in 51 years, the top four shut out the rest of the tour in the semi-finals. Sabalenka’s comeback victory against Linda Noskova, the 21-year-old Wimbledon champion, was one of the best matches of the year and she will eventually reflect on how well she recovered just to reach the final after such a nightmare summer.

Elena Rybakina dealt spectacularly with so many obstacles: the No 1 ranking, an achilles injury and one of the toughest possible draws to win the title. Her level on hard courts over the past year has been incredible and her quiet, reserved nature is the perfect foil to the intense extroversion of Sabalenka.

Meanwhile, Zheng Qinwen’s back-to-back comebacks from 0-5 to 7-5 in the third set of her third-round match against Madison Keys, and then in the first set of her fourth-round match against Iga Swiatek, were astonishing and she greatly deserved her dramatic return to the big stage. Iva Jovic and Alexandra Eala showed relentless competitiveness can sit comfortably with strong friendship as they battled into the night. A year after the pitiful state of her serve reduced her to tears on the court, Coco Gauff’s semi-final run was a reflection of her great progress.

Conversely, 2026 has been a miserable year for men’s tennis, primarily due to the shocking amount of injuries sustained by younger players. The difficulties of Carlos Alcaraz and Jannik Sinner are only the tip of the iceberg: Jack Draper, Holger Rune, Lorenzo Musetti, Arthur Fils and João Fonseca have all missed a significant amount of the past year. Even those who competed in New York are still working through the consequences of missing so much action.

The men’s draw still produced one of the memorable sporting moments of the year courtesy of a special champion. At 3.40am on Wednesday, after Ben Shelton’s monumental victory against Alcaraz, the Spaniard finally made his exit from Ashe. He had pushed himself to the limit for 4hr 28min, vomiting repeatedly, only to lose by narrow margins in a fifth set tie-break. However, after being away for four and a half months because of a wrist injury and unsure about how his body would react upon his return, he was finally able to again participate in the sport he loves and he left the court feeling like himself. As Alcaraz walked through the tunnel leading to the locker room, a place that had seen so many tears, his face broke out into a wide, joyful smile.

It’d be a great opportunity for you.’ I absolutely loved the job. They were the things I passed on to Flem. And I also thought for the group, for English cricket, he would be absolutely the right person to take this team forward.”

England will start the series against Sri Lanka without Phil Salt, Jacob Bethell and Sam Curran for fitness reasons, with Jofra Archer rested after his recent exertions with the Test side and with Brydon Carse absent for disciplinary reasons. In the viral commercial for Novig, which was viewed more than 22 million times in the first two days of its release, Sweeney’s nude body is covered by footballs, basketballs, and other sports equipment, as she tells users they can bet on “just sports”. The advert has led to a storm of protest led by the British sprinter Amy Hunt, who won four European Championship gold medals last month. After finishing fourth in the 200m at the World Athletics Ultimate Championship on Sunday evening, Hunt said: “Sydney Sweeney, this is what women in sport look like: 21.4. Muscles. That was a reference to Melissa Jefferson-Wooden’s winning time of 21.47 seconds, the fourth-fastest women’s 200m, and Hunt went on to reveal the painful realities she and other sports stars faced. “When you’re a woman in sport, it’s not pretty,” she said. “It’s not glamorous. “There’s some low moments. Even turning up to this championship, my period started yesterday, so that’s not really ideal, and that’s not ever what you try to really plan for.”
