Bob Mackie, costume designer to stars daring to be noticed, dies aged 87

The Guardian Mon, 14 Sep 2026 18:39:17 GMT

Famous for his flamboyant outfits, he helped celebrities including Cher, Tina Turner and Elton John cause a stir

Bob Mackie, the costume designer behind some of the most sexy and glamorous outfits worn by celebrities in the past 50 years, has died at the age of 87.

“He lived his 87 years to the fullest, fulfilling his dream of being a fashion and costume designer, which is all he ever wanted to do,” read a statement posted on his Instagram account. “His genius and extraordinary designs will live on forever, continuing to bring beauty into this world.”

Mackie’s work can be seen in the wardrobes of stars ranging from Marilyn Monroe to Carol Burnett, Liza Minnelli, Elton John, Dolly Parton, Tina Turner and – perhaps most memorably – Cher. He designed the ‘naked’ dress the singer wore to attend the Met Gala in 1975, the midriff-baring outfit with an oversized Mohawk headdress she wore to the Oscars in 1986 and the transparent body stocking she wore for the If I Could Turn Back Time video in 1989.

The Met Gala outfit has since become a reference for a younger generation. Kim Kardashian wore a dress modelled on it for the same event in 2015.

More recently, Taylor Swift wore one of Mackie’s original Jubilee! cabaret costumes on the cover of her 12th studio album, The Life of a Showgirl, while Sabrina Carpenter and Zendaya have also worn archival looks by the designer. In 2024, the singer Miley Cyrus paid an undisclosed sum to buy the Mackie tasseled mini dress she had worn to perform at the Grammys.

Last year at an auction, Cher’s “naked” bodysuit fetched $57,600 (£42,600), seven times its estimated price, while a silver and gold fringed bodysuit with lamé wings that Mackie designed for Tina Turner for a 1977 performance sold for $19,200 (£14,200).

The designer first began working with Cher for The Sonny and Cher show in the 1960s and remained a collaborator for decades. Cher has paid tribute to his contribution to her career, saying that without Mackie “I would have been a peacock without feathers”.

Mackie’s first notable design has another connection to Kardashian – as assistant to designer Jean Louis, he sketched the dress Marilyn Monroe wore to sing Happy Birthday to president John F Kennedy in 1962. Kardashian wore the original dress to the Met Gala in 2022 – to the disapproval of much of the fashion world, who thought it should be preserved. Mackie was one of the people who spoke out. “I thought it was a big mistake,” he said to Entertainment Weekly. “It was designed for [Monroe]. Nobody else should be seen in that dress.”

In 1963, he began to work on The Judy Garland Show, and met his collaborator and partner Ray Aghayan. Work for the Supremes, and then Diana Ross, followed. The duo were nominated for an Oscar for the costumes Ross wore in the 1973 Billie Holliday biopic Lady Sings the Blues.

Mackie’s motto was “dare to be noticed” and his costumes certainly gained attention for the people wearing them. Elton John’s duck costume, worn in 1980, has become notorious. But the designs also sometimes made points. Cher’s outfit for the Oscars in 1986 was so flamboyant because the star felt she was snubbed for her performance in Mask and wanted to take revenge when she was presenting an award.

Speaking to the New York Times a year later she said: “OK, you can go in a simple black dress and be just like everyone else. But then I decided, I’m going to remind them of what they don’t like about me.” Mackie obliged with his creation.

Turner’s “flame” dress, worn in 1977 after her split from her abusive partner and musical collaborator, Ike, turned the star into a gloriously unsubtle phoenix rising from the ashes.

The designer hasn’t always been harmonious with his clients. His work with Cher had tensions. In 2018, talking to the Guardian about the raunchy Turn Back Time outfit, he said he thought it was “vulgar and horrid”. “I told her: please, I don’t want any credit for this,” he said. In 2019, he described Garland as “a big handful” and said he refused to design costumes for a recent Cher tour. “I’m in touch with clients only when they need clothes,” he said. “I never want to be their best friend.”

Mackie diversified beyond costume design. He launched a clothing line in 1982 and made Bob Mackie collectible Barbies. Working with QVC from 1999, Mackie’s aesthetic has been utilised on everything from fragrance to luggage to high-end jewellery – and in 2009 he appeared as a guest judge on RuPaul’s Drag Race.

Mackie gained plaudits for his unique take on glamour in recent years. The Fashion Institute of Technology staged the Unmistakably Bob exhibition in 1999, and he received the prestigious Geoffrey Beene CFDA Lifetime Achievement award in 2019. He was front and centre of the Diva exhibition at London’s V&A in 2023, with Turner’s flame dress a highlight. The exhibition showed how Mackie’s design accentuated Turner’s showmanship and made her performance even more memorable. This was, ultimately, Mackie’s talent. “I’m very serious about this,” he said in 2018. “It’s not just flamboyant, crazy stuff. It’s all very worked out.”

Several celebrities paid tribute to the designer on social media.

Carpenter wrote on Instagram that she felt “so lucky to have met Bob.

“His one of a kind creations have inspired and brought so much happiness and confidence to my world and they will continue to always x Mackie girl forever.”

Kathy Lennon, a member of the vocal group The Lennon Sisters, described Mackie as “always so welcoming and complimentary when we went to his amazing costume showroom.”

“In a sea of ego, he seemed to have none,” Elton John wrote on Instagram. “One of the most courteous, incredible people I ever had the pleasure of working with.”

The Canadian model Coco Rocha said it was an “enormous privilege” to work with Mackie and wear his designs.

“There are designers whose work defines a moment, and then there are those rare few whose imagination teaches fashion something for generations,” Rocha said on Instagram. “Bob was one of them. His clothes had wit, drama, fantasy and joy.”

The Guardian view on Reform UK: crypto billionaires must be stopped from undermining democracy

The Guardian Mon, 14 Sep 2026 18:13:14 GMT

The vast sums given to Nigel Farage’s party in recent days must lead to action on political funding

The staggering sums gifted to Reform UK over the weekend have transformed the context for the representation of the people bill making its way through parliament. The announcement of two £36m donations from Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne, both crypto billionaires who have lived abroad, makes Andy Burnham’s decision not to impose a limit on political donations – a move he supported before becoming prime minister – look even more misguided. Fortunately the House of Lords still has the chance to amend the bill. It should take it by imposing meaningful limits on both political donations and party spending.

It is unclear whether either man meets the criteria set out in the Rycroft review into foreign influence in politics. It set a maximum of £100,000 per annum for people who have not been in the UK for at least a year. Mr Delo previously lived in Hong Kong while Mr Harborne is based partly in Thailand; Nigel Farage said on Monday that he does not know the details of their movements. While ministers will view the prospect of a legal fight over eligibility with trepidation, they must do what it takes to ensure rules are met.

Reform UK’s support has fallen since a year ago, when polls showed it ahead of Labour, and again since May when it won more than 1,400 seats in local elections. After a summer dominated by investigations of its finances, and with the police widening their inquiries to include footage, aired on Channel 4, of officials apparently discussing ways to get around electoral law, Nigel Farage’s unfavourability rating has hit a 10-year high. But while this reversal of fortune has brought relief to opponents, there is no room for complacency. In 2024, 34% of votes secured a huge majority for Labour. The danger of a Farage premiership and all that it could mean for UK politics and civil society remains real.

Mr Farage no longer advertises his closeness to Donald Trump in the way he once did. But he shares the US president’s enthusiasm for crypto currencies, which is part of a wider agenda of aggressive financial deregulation. Last year he told a conference that he wants to turn the UK into “the world’s premier hub for cryptocurrency”. No wonder that Mr Harborne appears to be competing to be the party’s top supporter with Mr Delo – who was pardoned by Mr Trump following a 2022 conviction for failing to implement adequate anti‑money laundering controls.

The Rycroft review focused on foreign influence for good reason; it is for UK voters to choose their government. But ministers must look beyond the narrow question of outside interference. As well as donation and campaign spending caps, they should regulate party expenditure across the electoral cycle. Otherwise mega-rich donors can pay for years of polling, advertising, data and staff, before election-period limits apply.

A statement from unions is expected to signal a change of heart and support for a cap on donations. Ministers will need to find a carve-out protecting contributions from their members. A mechanism to prevent charities becoming a back door for rich individuals to fund parties is also needed. Democracy is undermined when the vastly wealthy make politics look like an auction, upending norms built up over decades. It is entirely wrong that two wealthy individuals should be able to spend their way to such an influential role in Britain’s political life.

The Guardian view on the united Ireland debate: shifting dynamics need to be treated with caution

The Guardian Mon, 14 Sep 2026 18:11:31 GMT

Donald Trump’s blithe comments at the weekend were characteristically unhelpful. A careful and considered discussion on the subject has yet to begin

A decade ago, the Democratic Unionist party (DUP) viewed Brexit as a potential gamechanger in the struggle to resist future pressure for a united Ireland. As the author and journalist Fintan O’Toole wrote in an essay published last year, the DUP hoped that the 2016 referendum would deliver “a double exit. Brexit would not simply mean the UK’s departure from the EU. It would also be an act of separation from the Republic. It would reverse the slow drift towards integration.” That proved to be, to put it mildly, a deeply flawed judgment.

The direction of travel since 2016 has instead been the opposite. Rather than leading to a hard border between Northern Ireland and Ireland, which would have disastrously undermined the Good Friday agreement, the UK’s divorce agreement from Brussels eventually placed one in the Irish Sea. The logic of further economic integration between north and south within the EU’s single market was reinforced.

At the same time, demographic change has meant that people with a Catholic background now outnumber those with a Protestant one in Northern Ireland, changing the political calculus. In 2022, Sinn Féin won a historic victory in Stormont elections, leading to Michelle O’Neill’s appointment as the first nationalist first minister. On Monday, during a meeting with the heads of the UK’s other devolved nations, Ms O’Neill welcomed off-the-cuff remarks by Donald Trump during an unofficial visit to Ireland, in which he said he would “love” to see unification. The US president’s comments, she claimed, reflected the fact “that there is a growing conversation around constitutional change”.

That is undoubtedly the case. But it is a debate that has barely begun, and one which needs to be conducted with care and caution. The 1998 Good Friday agreement was intentionally vague about the criteria for holding a border poll. Successive governments in London and Dublin have since preferred to concentrate on promoting and developing cross-border co-operation.

Given the history, and the level of political risk involved, that was a sensible strategy. But the dynamics of the debate have shifted. Mr Trump’s blithe remarks followed hard on the heels of an early spat between Ms O’Neill and Andy Burnham, after the prime minister said during a visit to Belfast that a poll on a united Ireland was “off the table”.

In the short and medium term, Mr Burnham’s position makes sense. Sinn Féin’s commitment to a referendum on Irish unity by 2030 is wildly unrealistic. But for all sides, sleepwalking into a vote without adequate preparation is equally unpalatable. In the absence of a proper debate, commitment to unity in the Irish republic is broadbased but shallow. In Northern Ireland a disturbing revival of tensions over Orange Order marches in Catholic areas suggests deepening polarisation, fuelled by ongoing political dysfunction at Stormont.

A sober, lengthy and detailed public conversation is required over what form unification might take, and the possible trade-offs involved. In an interview with the Guardian last month, the former prime minister Gordon Brown suggested that “of course, in the long term, Ireland will be united”. Unlike Mr Trump, though, he added a significant rider. Reaching that outcome would be “a long process where people have got to come together and find a way of agreeing. Basically, that is the issue: whether people can actually agree.” Leaders on all sides of the debate should heed that caveat.

Andrew Davies admits to drawing on ‘stimulating’ Made in Chelsea for Jane Austen adaptation

The Guardian Mon, 14 Sep 2026 17:41:06 GMT

Screenwriter points to parallels between two worlds while academic says some of author’s characters ‘would make perfect reality show contestants’

If Jane Austen’s novels run on closed social worlds, courtship rituals, status anxiety, gossip and relentless scrutiny of who’s coupling with who, it follows that the obvious contemporary equivalent would be reality television.

That’s according to Andrew Davies, the writer who has spent decades modernising British period dramas.

Speaking on Radio 4’s Today programme on Monday, Davies revealed that he had been watching Made in Chelsea while working on an adaptation of Austen’s unfinished novel The Watsons.

“It’s stimulating really for relationships and ideas,” he said of the Channel 4 series, which follows the relationship dramas and social rivalries of affluent young residents of west London. “These young men and women in The Watsons, for example, are very analogous to Made in Chelsea.”

Davies, whose memoir An Unsuitable Boy: A Life in Scripts is out this week, is responsible for the legendary image of Colin Firth as Mr Darcy emerging from a lake in a wet shirt in his 1995 BBC adaptation of Pride and Prejudice, which went some way to injecting Austen into Bridget Jones, written by Helen Fielding around the time it aired. His approach, he said, had been about “bringing out the sex that’s inherent in Austen”.

He has previously described his 2019 adaptation of Sanditon as “Love Island” in Austen’s world and talked about whether Charlotte would “friend-zone” someone or experience a “fanny flutter”. Meanwhile Rose Williams, who starred in the series, said she believed “Austen would probably write something satirical about Love Island if she were alive today”.

Joe Bray, an Austen scholar and professor of English at the University of Sheffield, said of the author: “Jane Austen was a shrewd observer of the fashionable manners and fads adopted by the young … and the plots of most of her novels are driven by sexual attraction and/or secret liaisons and engagements.”

The Steele sisters in Sense and Sensibility, he suggested, “would make perfect reality show contestants”.

Austen also pioneered a way of representing the unspoken thoughts and feelings of her female characters that can be difficult to translate to screen. But Bray noted that Austen herself loved gossiping about neighbours and acquaintances in letters to her sister Cassandra. “I can’t say for certain whether or not she would be a viewer of Made in Chelsea or Love Island,” he said, “but … she would be interested at least!”

An academic essay on Made in Chelsea described the programme as a “kind of homage” to Austen, arguing that its subject was the “courtship rituals” of young people with money and property, and compared its social world to Pride and Prejudice and Emma.

There is indeed a human link between Made in Chelsea and Netflix’s forthcoming Pride and Prejudice: the latter’s writer and executive producer, Dolly Alderton, began her career as a story producer on the reality show – where, she has said, her job involved turning the romantic entanglements of wealthy young Londoners into “a four-part comedy drama”.

It remains to be seen whether the Netflix series draws any inspiration from Made in Chelsea, but Reddit users have previously theorised about whether Alderton took inspiration from the reality show, or her TV adaptation of her memoir Everything I Know About Love. “Who do we think the character ‘Kyle’ is based off? I’m getting Spencer Matthews and Jamie Laing [both Made in Chelsea cast members],” one wrote.

In her 2016 modernisation of Pride and Prejudice, Eligible, novelist Curtis Sittenfeld’s transplanted the Bennets to contemporary Cincinnati and made Chip Bingley a former reality-TV star who had appeared on The Bachelor.

“Reality dating shows are so formulaic, and courtship in Austen’s time was rigid and proscriptive,” Sittenfeld said. In other words, reality TV provided a modern equivalent for Austen’s world of carefully prescribed romantic encounters; in place of the wealthy unmarried man arriving in the neighbourhood, there is the reality-TV bachelor whose romantic availability is already a matter of public interest.

That may explain the extraordinary portability of Austen, from Clueless, which transplanted Emma to 1990s LA, and Bridget Jones’s Diary to Fire Island, Persuasion and the forthcoming Sense and Sensibility.

John Mullan, a literature professor at University College London and historical and dialogue consultant on Bridgerton, identified another parallel.

“In Austen’s fiction, courtship mostly takes place under the eyes of others,” he said. “Young women and men who might fancy each other are very rarely alone.”

But, he added, there is a crucial difference: “What about propriety, restraint, repression? These are also key to Austen’s stories and characters.”

As Reform celebrates £72m in donations, tell me this: are you ready to see two rich men buy our democracy?

The Guardian Mon, 14 Sep 2026 17:19:46 GMT

It’s not just that Nigel Farage claimed his movement abhorred the super-rich. It’s also the obscenity of individuals seeking so much sway over who runs the country

As £72m in donations makes its way to Reform UK’s bank accounts, consider what Nigel Farage said on the eve of Britain’s vote to leave the European Union a decade ago. “This referendum is the people versus the establishment,” he declared. “It is the vested interest, it’s the rich, it’s the big business.”

Just two years ago, Farage assailed “an unholy alliance of big business, big banks and big government”. He is also the same man who, when he debated with the then Liberal Democrat leader, Nick Clegg, in 2014, claimed to “represent the mercantile, trading, entrepreneurial end of society”, while his opponent “represents big banks, big government and big business”.

To be clear, Farage’s political outfit is being bankrolled by two cryptobillionaires. One of them is Ben Delo, who once developed high-frequency trading systems for JP Morgan. That investment bank was a particular bete noire of Farage: when it backed the Remain campaign, he savaged “the unholy alliance of big banks and big politics”. The other is the Thailand-based cryptobillionaire Christopher Harborne, who gave Farage his pre-election £5m gift and provided two-thirds of Reform’s funding – until now, that is.

Neither of them is the plucky small merchant evoked by Farage’s rhetoric. The man who denounced banks buying political influence is now dependent on two wealthy figures from the world of finance. Predictably, Reform says its benefactors want “nothing” in return for their colossal donations. Yet the two businessmen who have just coughed up the biggest donations in British political history will surely be delighted with Reform’s plans to slash taxes on crypto assets and set up a “bitcoin reserve”.

The political fraud that is rightwing “populism” is quite something to behold. These movements claim to champion the little guy against the elites. Whether embodied by wealthy tycoon Donald Trump, whose relatives and friends are making a killing from his administration, or the privately educated millionaire ex-City broker Farage, the formula is straightforward. Dupe struggling people into believing their problems are caused by migrants, refugees and minorities – while championing the interests of the mega-rich who actually hold the power.

Sure, British democracy has always come with heavy caveats. Political parties and politicians have always received hefty donations from an economic elite that, to be clear, does not give money away without expecting a return. They can also rely on powerful lobbyists to advance their interests. Then there’s the “revolving door” through which politicians and civil servants leave public office for lucrative jobs with companies in the very industries they were previously responsible for overseeing and regulating. And there’s a British newspaper industry mostly owned by rich moguls with a vested interest in defending a status quo they profit from.

But these latest donations take the corruption of our democracy to a whole new level. That two donations to Reform in a single weekend now eclipse the total amount spent by all political parties at the last general election tells its own story. Indeed, these donations amount to about 14 times the total spent by Farage’s party at the last election – when, it should be noted, it won more than 4m votes, or one in seven votes cast.

The party can now pay for hundreds of full-time staff, build local political hubs and massively expand its polling and research infrastructure. Crucially, it can throw vast sums at digital advertising, which can be uniquely tailored to the interests and concerns of individual voters. We know from research in the US that digital ads can shift voting intention. The more money a political party has, the more it can afford to experiment until it finds the ads that work.

Indeed, all the evidence suggests that money wins votes. A recent peer-reviewed study examined every British general election between 1857 and 2017, and found a strong relationship between relative campaign spending and votes. Rich donors really do shower political parties with money for a reason. Reform’s mega-donations underline that democracy is for sale.

But could this spectacularly backfire? Reform is, after all, already embroiled in multiple controversies over gifts and donations from wealthy donors, and its ratings have taken a bad beating. Polling earlier this year found that 83% of Brits believe that “wealthy individuals use political donations to influence the government to further their own personal interests”. That figure was only four points lower among Reform voters, who were also nearly 10 times as likely to say they would view a party more favourably if it promised to cap donations as to view it less favourably.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

It would be naive, alas, to believe that this will finally burst the gilded Reform bubble. What it does do depends on what the national political conversation is about. Labour has had long enough in government to change the law to block such donations, and tragically Andy Burnham has retreated from his stated desire to cap them at £500,000.

But that would mean a Labour party that was determined to confront wealthy vested interests. Because Starmerism had no desire to replace an economic order rigged in favour of elites, it was unable to redirect anger away from the scapegoating of migrants. Instead, it simply replicated Farage’s xenophobia, which only ever legitimises the arguments of the anti-migrant right.

A different approach, based on redistributing wealth and power, would force a different conversation. So far, thanks to pressure from Zack Polanski’s Green party, Burnham has shifted some of the rhetoric. But if Labour were to, say, hike taxes on wealth in order to invest in crumbling services, it could pair that with a sustained attack on Farage as the plaything of wealthy vested interests.

Otherwise, the outrage over these donations will fade. The old poison will remain – and this time it comes with £72m behind it.

Owen Jones is a Guardian columnist. His latest book, The Fall of the West: How They Really Lost It, is released in October. Order your copy at the Guardian bookshop

Richard Tice rallies to the defence of Reform’s crypto ‘patriots’

The Guardian Mon, 14 Sep 2026 17:05:50 GMT

You can’t buy Dicky’s level of stupidity though it could be argued that Christopher Harborne and Ben Delo just have

Never in the field of British politics has so much been given to so many by so few. You’d have thought Nigel Farage would have wanted to explain Reform’s sudden windfall from Christopher Harborne and Ben Delo himself. To bask in the glory of the donations from two down-to-earth, anti-establishment crypto billionaires. Men who know what it’s like to graft, who know the meaning of an honest day’s work for an honest day’s pay.

There again, Nige is keen not to appear as a one-man band these days and he could do with some downtime to enjoy his own £5m handout. And besides, he’s got a police investigation into Reform party funding to worry about. Even so, it wasn’t the best of looks to send Richard Tice out on to the morning media round. Dicky may have his talents, but he keeps them well concealed. His main talent is the unfortunate ability to make Honest Bob Jenrick sound trustworthy. But he does always leave you guessing. Is he being wilfully stupid or is he naturally that half witted?

Dicky began with a howl of protest. No rules had been broken. He made that sound as if it came as a surprise to him. I guess that’s an easy mistake for anyone to make. Everything was in the rules as they exist. Labour was mounting a coup against Reform for having passed legislation through the Commons that would prevent donors living overseas from giving more than £100,000 until they had lived in the UK for more than a calendar year, backdated to March 2026. You’d have thought Nige might have clocked this. But he probably hadn’t been in Westminster that day. And you can’t trust Dicky to be over the details.

“Our money comes with no demands,” Dicky told Nick Robinson on the Today programme. Harborne and Delo were patriots. All they wanted was to save the country from being ruined by socialists and the rightwing Tories. Quite where he thought Reform fitted in on this particular continuum wasn’t clear. Presumably in the centre ground of British politics. Ordinary men and women who want to rescue their country from the do-goodery of the RNLI.

“Patriots” was doing some heavy lifting here. Harborne had decamped to Thailand in the 90s, had become a Thai citizen in 2011 and had taken a Thai name. Now we learned that Dicky believed in dialectics. The more someone looked as if they were trying to put as much distance between themselves and the UK, the greater their commitment to the UK really was. Chris had just been playing very hard to get. The reality was he had been begging HMRC to ask him back so he could pay his fair share to the exchequer.

Fine, said Robinson. When did he move back to the UK and does he now pay UK tax? Dicky was understandably clueless. He had no idea he was going to be asked whether Harborne complied with the law as it was going through parliament. I’m not his tax adviser, he protested, though if he was he would make sure he paid as little as possible. Dicky has always been upfront in his belief that only the little people pay tax. And as for Harborne’s whereabouts, he wasn’t his diary secretary. He just telepathically knew that Chris had complied with the law as it was and as it was proposed.

It was the same with Delo. No man had ever loved his country more. From Hong Kong. Who wouldn’t want to receive money from a billionaire who had been convicted in the US for failing to comply with money-laundering laws and had been pardoned by Donald Trump? Dicky had no idea when Ben had come back to the country. That sort of level of detail was well above his pay grade. He was just here for the front-of-house stuff. The meet and greet. No one should expect any more from him than that.

Then the killer line. “I hope you will trust the word of our compliance team,” said Dicky. They would assure listeners everything was above board. So touching. So sweet. Up till now, no one had any idea Reform even had a compliance team. They certainly hadn’t been much in evidence while James Orr and Dan Jukes had been negotiating a possible £500,000 gift from an overseas donor. And in the taped conversation, which Nige insisted he hadn’t been listening to, Farage had said, “it’s all above board”.

So, if it’s all the same, we won’t be taking the word of an imaginary compliance team. Nick pressed on. What did Dicky think had attracted two crypto billionaires to a party that had promised to cut taxes on crypto, to limit regulation of the industry and had threatened to remove the governor of the Bank of England if he didn’t play ball?

Dicky couldn’t quite put his finger on it. But he thought it was probably something to do with them really caring about a £500 tax break. And the pleasure of paying for Nige’s hideous suit. Champagne and oysters all round.

There was just time for Robinson to point out that, far from getting nothing for their donations, the two men had already got everything they wanted and more. “Not at all,” Dicky insisted. Because Reform had promised to deregulate and cut tax before the two men had handed over the £72m. Where can you go with someone as dim as Dicky? A tale told by an idiot, signifying nothing. You can’t buy Dicky’s level of stupidity. Though Harborne and Delo just have.

It was left to Farage himself to clear up Tice’s mess later in the day in a BBC interview. Well, sort of. Yes, Delo and Harborne’s donations probably wouldn’t meet the necessary deadlines for the legislation going through parliament. But you couldn’t blame Reform for taking the cash. Rather it was the fault of the government for putting in place regulations that Reform might not now be able to get round. As so often with Nige, there was always someone else to blame.

Not that Labour was immune from a little hypocrisy. It had been Burnham who had tried to bury the plan to limit donations to all parties. Something the unions had pushed back against. But the £72m has rather concentrated everyone’s minds. Once the current legislation was through parliament there would still be a good year to pass another law to impose a cap. Down in Brighton, Angela Rayner wanted the TUC to know she was on their side. There was no equivalence between Labour funding from the unions and money from two crypto billionaires. Politics could be bought. Just by the right sort of people.

‘A coin flip’: on the campaign trail as Brazil’s far right edges back to power

Neck-and-neck with Lula in polls, Flávio Bolsonaro fires up his base in the bellwether state of Minas Gerais – starting at the scene of his father’s stabbing

A giant banner of Brazil’s incarcerated former president Jair Bolsonaro fluttered in the morning breeze as his eldest son, Flávio, touched down at an airfield on the fringe of a city that will soon help decide the future of one of the biggest democracies on earth.

“Brazil is rudderless. Brazil has no president and Brazil needs a president – and that president is Flávio Bolsonaro,” the far-right senator declared as he waded into the flock of supporters who had gathered to welcome him to Juiz de Fora, one of the largest cities in the battleground state of Minas Gerais.

With less than a month before nearly 159 million Brazilians choose their next leader on 4 October, the election appears on a knife-edge, with the incumbent leftwing president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, and his challenger, Flávio Bolsonaro, neck-and-neck in the polls.

Bolsonaro’s campaign appears to have seized the momentum in recent weeks amid a slew of corruption scandals involving Lula’s son and the supreme court. That has prompted despair among progressives who fear their country could fall back into the hands of a radical rightwing movement that tried to grab power after the then-president, Jair Bolsonaro, lost the 2022 election to Lula.

Last September, Jair Bolsonaro received a 27-year jail sentence for spearheading that botched coup – a verdict supporters insist was unjust. But the ex-president and his accomplices are likely to be freed if his son wins power – a prospect that delights the hardcore Bolsonaristas who turned out to greet Flávio Bolsonaro wearing yellow football shirts and headbands reading: “Lula out!”

“Today is a moment of joy,” said Ulisses Lima, 50, a cybersecurity specialist with a Jesus Christ pendant around his neck. “Flávio represents change. He represents Brazil’s rescue from this socialist abyss we’ve spent so long warning about,” Lima added as supporters waited for the former president’s heir to arrive.

Nearby, another devotee, José Caldeira, fell to his knees and begged for divine intervention to get Bolsonaro out of house arrest. “God, free this nation! Amnesty and freedom for Bolsonaro!” Caldeira bellowed, raising his hands towards the sky.

A third man, Davi Frederico, held a banner celebrating Donald Trump, who has been accused of trying to swing the election in Bolsonaro’s favour through economic and diplomatic pressure. “Make Liberals Cry Again,” it said.

Juiz de Fora, an industrial and university city traditionally associated with the left, is also a key location for Brazil’s hard right. The city’s army headquarters was the launchpad for the 1964 coup that plunged Brazil into two decades of military rule. And it was in Juiz de Fora, on the eve of the 2018 election, that Jair Bolsonaro was stabbed in the gut while campaigning – an attack widely believed to have helped the former paratrooper seal his victory.

Bolsonaro’s shock win ushered in what, from a progressive perspective, were four abysmal years. Destruction of the Amazon rainforest and gun ownership skyrocketed, hundreds of thousands died during a Covid outbreak Bolsonaro was accused of mishandling, and the president’s authoritarian rhetoric and attacks on Brazil’s electronic voting system culminated in the 8 January 2023 riots in Brasília. The supreme court later called those disturbances part of a plot to “annihilate” the country’s democracy.

But the Bolsonaros still enjoy abundant support, and that devotion was visible as Flávio Bolsonaro’s motorcade crept towards the high street where his father was ambushed eight years ago.

“Let’s get the left out! Let’s get these motherfuckers out!” one elderly woman shrieked as the senator passed by on top of a sound truck stamped with the word: “Jesus”. Other fans, many senior citizens, waved Brazil flags from windows or stood on the sidewalk flashing victory signs with their hands.

“Barring some kind of leftwing trickery, Flávio Bolsonaro can already be considered president. All you have to do is take a look at the streets and social media,” claimed Nikolas Ferreira, an influential far-right congressman from Minas Gerais who has more than 9 million TikTok followers.

Alongside the enthusiasm, there were glimpses of the revulsion many Brazilians feel for the former president. One leftwinger took to his balcony with a loudhailer to taunt the Bolsonaristas as they paraded through town. “Trump! Trump! Get my daddy out of jail!” the dissenter jeered in reference to the US president’s attempts to help Bolsonaro escape punishment.

Minas Gerais, a mountainous mining and agricultural region that is larger than France and has 21 million inhabitants, is Brazil’s bellwether state. Since democracy returned in the 1980s, no candidate has won the presidency without triumphing here. In 2018, Jair Bolsonaro beat Lula’s candidate in Minas by more than 1.7m votes. Four years later, Lula reclaimed the state by fewer than 50,000. After landing in Minas last week, Flávio Bolsonaro said he was confident of clawing back the swing state, with one recent poll putting him ahead there.

“[Lula] is a president who you look at and see the past,” the 45-year-old senator said of his 80-year-old adversary. “With Flávio you can be sure that when people look at him, they see a modern government and a government of the future.”

Thomas Traumann, a political analyst who has written a book about his polarised country, said the election was too close to call. “It’s a coin flip,” said Traumann, who believed an unexpected scandal or last-minute “black swan” event could swing the election either way. On Friday, it emerged that Flávio Bolsonaro had been placed under police investigation over suspicions of corruption involving the funding of a big-budget biopic telling the story of the assassination attempt against his father in Juiz de Fora.

For progressive voters, the vision for a Flávio Bolsonaro administration laid out during his visit to Minas is the stuff of nightmares. “I think Flávio Bolsonaro’s presidency is going to be Jair Bolsonaro 2.0,” said Bruno Engler, a Bolsonarista lawmaker from Minas’ capital, Belo Horizonte.

Engler believed a top priority would be zero-tolerance policing, with the younger Bolsonaro pledging an iron-fisted crackdown on criminals his father has compared to cockroaches. “Thugs who don’t surrender will be arrested or neutralised,” Engler vowed, predicting gun laws would be loosened.

Speaking on the street corner where his father was knifed, Flávio Bolsonaro vowed to pack Brazil’s 11-member supreme court with five conservative judges “who are against abortion [and] against drugs”. “We’re going to give the streets back to the Brazilian people … We’re going to lower the age of criminal responsibility. We are going to introduce chemical castration for rapists,” shouted the candidate, who wore a bullet-proof vest.

Those pledges prompted whoops of excitement from the crush of supporters below Bolsonaro’s truck. Dozens ofmobile phones captured the candidate’s every word. But amid the rightwing rejoicing there was fear and trepidation, too.

Lennon César, a law student and leftwing activist who had come to confront Bolsonaro’s fans, voiced incredulity that less than four years after Jair Bolsonaro’s failed power grab, tens of millions of Brazilians seemed poised to vote for his son.

“We were the victims of an attempted coup – and his father was the perpetrator,” recalled César, 28. “It’s terrifying. And the thing that worries me most is that the general public doesn’t really seem to get what’s happening. Brazilians have short memories when it comes to the past.”

As a black, gay man, César felt particular dread at the prospect of a second Bolsonaro presidency, given the patriarch’s hostility to minorities.

César vowed to vote for Lula, Brazil’s first working-class president, calling him the only leader who paid attention to the poor. “If today I’m studying for a law degree it’s because one of Lula’s government programmes allowed me to achieve that,” he said, warning: “These people … might destroy it all.”

A few blocks away, a graffiti artist had spray painted their own message of disapproval on to the facade of Bolsonaro’s Juiz de Fora HQ. “Facists [sic],” it read.

Why has university become such a scam?

The Guardian Mon, 14 Sep 2026 16:55:50 GMT

Graduates are leaving with an average debt of £53,000 – while entry-level jobs plummet. It’s time for politicians to stop burying their heads in the sand

It wasn’t in relation to university that I first came across the organisation Rethink Repayment, which campaigns for a fairer settlement on student debt. I was looking into the astronomical numbers of young people who still live with their parents. It’s now more than a third of young men and more than a fifth of young women, statistics that get even crunchier when you realise that “young” describes anyone under 35.

There were various reasons – some had gone home after a health crisis, some really liked their parents, some were battling unemployment, but the single unifying theme was student debt. Those on incomes too low to start repaying couldn’t make rent; those in the lower repayment bracket (an annual income of £25,000 or thereabouts, depending on your loan plan) still couldn’t make rent, because they were spending 9% of their income repaying. And those on more than £50,000 were keeping less than 50p in every pound they earn because of their marginal tax rate. It’s always been sold to students when they take on this debt that it won’t count against their mortgage raising capacity, which technically it won’t – but any affordability check by a mortgage company or letting agent will factor in the monthly repayments.

It feels tactless to bring this up, just as a fresh wave of students heads off, with bigger, more exciting things on their minds than long-term debt. Yet it also feels remiss not to mention the fact that they’re being absolutely had. Florence, 29, who works as a solicitor in commercial litigation, is still living at home. She told me: “A lot of the time I’m reviewing contracts, and saying: ‘This is enforceable, sue them.’ The holes in what we were told are shocking. If student loans had come from an institutional lender, we would have a class action lawsuit.”

Without lingering on the unedifying details, such as how we’re all feeling about Nick Clegg nowadays, a quick recap on what the debate around student fees looked like when they were first hiked to £9,000 in 2012. There was a lot of anxiety about whether the government would ever get its money back, or whether a huge amount of this debt would have to be written off – what we didn’t factor in back then was that, this being the government, they could make the rules. If they wanted the interest on student loans to be set at the Retail Prices Index (RPI) measure of inflation, plus up to 3%, they could simply snap their fingers and make it so. We talked a lot, too, about what those capped fees meant for universities – 10 years ago, £9,000 wasn’t enough for some courses but it was more than they needed for “classroom subjects” (a lot of humanities), which could then cross-subsidise. Now, with fees only increased to £9,790 in more than a decade, they often don’t even cover humanities courses – so worries about the sheer viability of what was previously one of the nation’s most successful sectors were well founded.

The students themselves were almost a side issue in this debate: the promise was that the debt would be more than offset by their increased earning capacity, once they had a degree, and, anyway, wouldn’t affect them until they could well afford it. This has turned out to be wildly untrue. Graduates are leaving with an average burden of £53,000, four or five times what it was in 2009, and the interest rates mean they can spend years repaying without making a dent in that amount. Graduate vacancies, meanwhile, were down 45% in August, compared with the same month last year, which is casually blamed on AI wiping out entry level jobs. Responsibility would be better situated with employers, who are choosing short-term cost-saving over their duty to their own companies, their society and the future.

It’s one thing to deprioritise the younger generation, it’s another to straight up scam them. I don’t want to tell any political party its business, but the one that makes a better offer than “pretend the problem doesn’t exist” stands to make enormous headway, and not just with the under-35s.

Zoe Williams is a Guardian columnist

Sweden’s political parties launch coalition talks as both blocs try to secure power

The Guardian Mon, 14 Sep 2026 16:47:25 GMT

Centre-left bloc led by Social Democrats has narrow lead with 95% of vote counted, but faces internal policy battle

Sweden’s political parties have launched coalition negotiations as the Social Democrats leader, Magdalena Andersson, started the long and difficult process of trying to form a new government.

Full results from Sunday’s election are not expected until after overseas votes are counted on Wednesday, but with 95% of the votes counted, the Social Democrats and the centre-left bloc had a narrow but growing lead of 176 seats to the right-leaning parties’ 173.

After losing support for the first time since they were founded, the far-right Sweden Democrats, who were hoping to enter government for the first time, appear to be out of the picture. But many of its policy ideas – on immigration laws, integration and crime – have become mainstream, including in the centre-left.

Both Andersson and the outgoing centre-right prime minister, Ulf Kristersson, of the Moderates have each said they want to explore possible coalition options to secure power.

After a long election night during which there was just one seat between the two blocs, Social Democrat leaders met Andersson on Monday morning at the party’s Stockholm headquarters.

Questions remain as to whether the bloc is willing to work with the Left party (Vänsterpartiet), which the Centre party has previously ruled out.

The Social Democrats press secretary, Tobias Baudin, said he had been in contact with colleagues from opposition parties and called for the resignation of Kristersson, who led the rightwing Tidö coalition government with the support of the Sweden Democrats.

“Now the voters have had their say and they have given him a failing grade for himself and his government,” Baudin told the Swedish broadcaster SVT, adding: “He should resign himself. In fact it doesn’t matter, if he doesn’t resign he will be removed. How he does it is up to him.

The Centre party said that in talks with the Social Democrats it would be seeking a government with a “desire for political stability” and a “clear centre-right character” with no “fringe politics”.

The Social Democrat Morgan Johansson, who under the last Social Democrat-led government was deputy prime minister, said the Centre party’s announcement was a positive development and that overall there were “good prospects”.

All of the left-leaning parties want a change of government, he said. “That is the starting point. I don’t think anyone wants us to end up in a situation where blockages lead to a new election.”

Meanwhile, Kristersson appears to be keeping his options open.

On Sunday night he said the result could lead to a “complicated government formation, where it ends remains to be seen”. On Monday, before a meeting with his fellow Tidö coalition leaders, he declined to elaborate, saying he would wait for a full result before having conversations. “If all the red lines remain then Sweden won’t have a government at all,” he added. “I plan to pursue a number of possibilities that may exist.”

The Liberals and Christian Democrats have both said they will not work with the Social Democrats.

After the overseas votes are counted on Wednesday, the final election results are not expected until the weekend.

The new parliament will meet for the first time on 28 September and the earliest date that the speaker can suggest a prime minister is 29 September, but talks could take considerably longer. If, when parliament votes for a prime minister candidate, more than half say no, then the speaker must find a new candidate. If there are four failed votes there will automatically be a new election.

After the 2022 election, it took 37 days to form a government; in 2018 it took 134 days to form a new coalition.

Fredrik Furtenbach, the senior political correspondent at Sveriges Radio (Radio Sweden), said: “I think it will end with either the Left or Centre party having to give way. It might take several failed prime minister votes first.” But he does not believe the Social Democrats and Moderates, who he describes as “traditional archenemies”, will end up working together. “You cannot share the position of prime minister.”

Keeping women out of prison must be the focus

The Guardian Mon, 14 Sep 2026 16:14:44 GMT

Readers respond to an editorial on overcrowded jails and plans to convert parts of the women’s prison estate for use by men

Your editorial (The Guardian view on the prisons crisis: moving men into women’s jails is not the answer, 10 September) is right to argue that the prison capacity crisis cannot be solved through a series of short-term fixes. Victims need confidence that the government has a credible long-term strategy for the criminal justice system, not another piecemeal intervention designed to buy time.

I share your concern about the pressures facing probation services. There are also legitimate questions about the impact on policing, but we cannot discuss the prisons crisis without confronting the crisis in our courts.

About one in five prisoners are now awaiting trial, often because cases are taking so long to be heard. Some defendants spend so long on remand that by the time they are sentenced, they are released from court, having effectively already served their sentence. Victims will rightly ask whether that is justice, and the public will rightly ask what it means for public safety.

The government points to the removal of foreign offenders as part of the solution to prison overcrowding. Yet a third are held on remand awaiting their day in court due to a court system in crisis.

Prisons, courts, probation and policing are interconnected. The government cannot hope to resolve the prisons crisis if it does not also resolve the crisis in our courts. Delays leave victims waiting years for justice, drive up the remand population and place further pressure on an overcrowded prison estate. As victims’ commissioner, I need assurances that the prime minister is focused on pursuing a strategy for the whole justice system, not simply responding to the latest emergency. Claire Waxman Victims’ commissioner for England and Wales

We are a collective of women’s charities, frontline services and women with lived experience of prison. We saw first-hand the devastating impact that Holloway prison’s closure had 10 years ago. For 170 years, it was a paradoxical space – a place of trauma, but also a crucible of feminist resistance and home to dozens of frontline services. From the suffragettes to the activist Chris Tchaikovsky, women’s history unfolded there. Now it has been razed.

This invites the question: what could we build instead? Your editorial offers some answers when it references the Corston review. However, one crucial element is missing: women’s centres. These are spaces where women’s services are brought together under one roof, offering support with housing, domestic abuse, employment, childcare, therapy and more. They help women holistically, rather than simply fixing one area of their lives. Women in Prison reports that for every £1 invested in a women’s centre, £2.75 is saved.

Women’s centres stop women entering the criminal justice system, keep children out of care and relieve pressure on emergency services. We’ve spent a decade campaigning for one on the Holloway prison site. The public are supportive and building work is under way, but funding is still not secured.

If Andy Burnham wanted to pursue a visionary policy, he could champion a women’s centre programme across the UK, starting with the Holloway Women’s Building. Polly CreedHolloway Women’s Building Collective, London

Measures to reduce the number of women behind bars are long overdue, but it must be more than a short-term fix to try to free up capacity (Ministers propose converting female prison estate into cells for men, 7 September).

Women in, and leaving, prison face particular challenges. Many have also been victims of crime or have children they hope to be reunited with. Rates of homelessness are higher among women than men when they leave prison.

These challenges also lead to higher numbers of women being recalled to prison. Our analysis found that there was one recall for every four women under post-release supervision in the community in the first three months of this year, compared with one recall for every five men.

In some cases, recall will have been needed to protect the public. But in others, better community support could and should be put in place.

If the government is serious about a long-term reduction in the number of women in prison, it should start by ensuring that women leaving prison are supported to stay out. Enver SolomonChief executive, Nacro

The reported proposal to convert parts of the women’s prison estate to accommodate male prisoners may initially sound controversial, but the more important question is why so many women need to be imprisoned in the first place.

A pilot women’s court in Bristol offers a potentially much more constructive answer. By taking a trauma-informed, problem-solving approach, the court seeks to address the circumstances underlying offending – including domestic abuse, addiction, mental ill health and homelessness – while still holding women accountable for their crimes.

This seems preferable to the familiar cycle of short prison sentences, release and reoffending. It also recognises something often overlooked in the debate: imprisoning women can have consequences far beyond the offender herself. Many are mothers and primary carers, so custody can profoundly disrupt children’s lives and family relationships.

If the Bristol experiment demonstrates that intensive community supervision and properly funded support can reduce reoffending while keeping women safely out of prison, it deserves to be expanded.

The real test of a successful prison policy should not be whether we can find more cells, but whether we can reduce the need for them. Stuart HarringtonBurnham-on-Sea, Somerset

Middle-class parenting neglects life skills that are essential for students

The Guardian Mon, 14 Sep 2026 16:12:02 GMT

We owe it to our young people to teach them how to do laundry and prepare food, writes Melissa Scallan, while Pippa Keech recalls her son’s university halls baptism of fire

Zoe Williams’ university-bound son won’t be the only one among his peers not to know how, or indeed why, bed sheets are laundered (I went to Ikea with my son – and was confronted with my parenting failures, 8 September).

Modern day, middle-class parenting tends to direct kids away from domestic pursuits, focusing instead on academic achievements and sporting prowess or music grades, scouting activities and Duke of Edinburgh awards. With their waking hours consumed by so many outside interests, there’s little time for learning life skills such as cooking, cleaning and laundering.

I visit schools giving talks to sixth-form students about preparing for university. In advance, I invite the students to share any questions or concerns they may have. Alongside issues such as finding their future friends and whether they’ll cope academically, they often question how they’ll live independently. Many of them have never had to do a full supermarket shop, prepare a meal from scratch, wash a kitchen floor or iron a shirt.

They anticipate focusing on their studies and socialising with their flatmates, coursemates and people they meet through clubs and societies. They do worry about how they’ll also take care of themselves and how they’ll juggle everything.

We owe it to our young people to teach them essential life skills along the way – not just in the week before they head off to university – so they have one less thing to worry about. After all, conjuring up a decent chilli, cleaning a loo properly and washing a sheet without it shrinking, fading or changing shape, are lifelong useful skills. Melissa ScallanAuthor, Starting University

Five minutes after dropping my son off at his Birmingham halls of residence, we received a WhatsApp message: “I cut my hand on a knife when I opened the packaging. There’s quite a lot of blood. Any advice?” As we turned the car round, while rummaging for plasters in the glove box, we got another message. “It’s OK, my new flatmates have bandaged me up.” All six are still close mates, 10 years later. Pippa KeechLyndhurst, Hampshire

Severe mental illness and the risk of violence

The Guardian Mon, 14 Sep 2026 16:10:13 GMT

A new willingness to acknowledge the risk that some people with severe mental illnesses may become violent is welcomed by Prof John F Morgan

Your report of Sarah Hughes’s acknowledgment that mental health organisations have sometimes “softened the truth” about the relationship between serious mental illness and violence marks an important change in the public debate (Mental health groups have ‘failed to acknowledge’ risk of violence, says Mind chief, 5 September).

There is some historical irony here. Mind grew from the National Association for Mental Health, an organisation in which psychiatrists and other mental health professionals played an important part. From the 1970s onwards, Mind increasingly defined itself as an independent campaigning organisation and, at times, a vigorous critic of psychiatric practice and authority.

As a psychiatrist who previously chaired the Royal College of Psychiatrists group concerned with risk, and who gave evidence to the Nottingham inquiry, I have seen the consequences of our difficulty in discussing this subject plainly.

Psychiatrists have long had to hold two propositions together. The overwhelming majority of people with mental illness are not violent and should not be stigmatised as such. But some severe mental disorders, particularly when accompanied by factors such as substance misuse, disengagement from treatment or a previous history of violence, can materially increase risk. Acknowledging the second proposition does not contradict the first.

Indeed, avoiding discussion of risk for fear of stigma can itself have consequences for patients, families and the wider public. Properly resourced services, continuity of care, assertive follow-up and thoughtful risk assessment protect patients as well as others.

It is therefore significant that Mind is now prepared to say publicly that the mental health charity sector has sometimes been too reluctant to acknowledge an uncomfortable reality. This should not become an argument between psychiatry and its critics. It is an opportunity for clinicians, patients and campaigning organisations to recover a more mature position: opposing stigma while being equally willing to speak honestly about risk. Prof John F MorganConsultant psychiatrist, Harrogate, North Yorkshire

‘A double entendre in every crevice’: what, beyond near-naked tennis, is Sydney Sweeney’s game?

The Guardian Mon, 14 Sep 2026 16:05:08 GMT

With her new, semi-nude advert for sports site Novig, the actor cements her reputation as the anti-woke poster girl. But is it real – or just provocation with a soft porn gaze?

Bear with me here, but I’m beginning to suspect Sydney Sweeney is a very fine actor. It’s a skill she has been recognised for in the past, of course, winning nominations for Emmys for Euphoria and The White Lotus, but I mean it in a deeper sense, related to her work in advertising rather than drama – can she do more than play a role? Can she make you feel what she’s feeling?

In her “controversial” new ad for the sports prediction site Novig (the scare quotes are because, when you’re begging for controversy this hard, you shouldn’t just be handed it on a plate), she adopts the garb of various sports. Her face, body, aspect, gait and mien are all carefully configured to amp up the erotic overtones to the maximum degree, and yet the feeling that beams out of each image is: “This is really going to piss people off, and I couldn’t be more delighted.” Her expression is so speechful that you cannot help but share in some of her hellion joy.

In brief: the proposition of the betting site is that it’s only for betting on sports – no wars, no deaths, no politics, just sports. Even the captions, absent the Sweeney, are a red rag to a bull, since betting on wars and death is a disgusting and inhumane thing to do – the surge in people trying to spin cash out of deaths in Iran, in Ukraine, says something profound about where we’ve got to in late capitalism. Whatever that profound thing is, it’s definitely not funny.

However, we are where we are, and that’s not Sweeney’s concern. She is there to wrinkle out the double entendre from every conceivable crevice. Do spherical things remind you of breasts? What if I get these two American footballs and put them in front of my actual breasts? Would it help if I was naked to the waist? Ah, better still if I were wearing no clothes at all and only the footballs stood between me and my modesty? The age-old tennis shot, immortalised by the 80s Athena poster in which the viewer is invited to consider just how nearly they can see a player’s butt – well, that’s here, only this time minus the skirt.

Sweeney’s facial expressions are like a WikiHow gallery, “how to: soft-porn” – they often feel quite old-fashioned, pert or faux naive, more like 70s graphic novel erotica than modern, up-to-the-minute pornography. Yet, throughout, there is a layer of knowingness: “I know exactly how much I’m going to drive you mad, and why.”

Truthfully, it’s hard (as a card-carrying member of the wokerati, just out here in the world, trying to keep up) to figure out what the fundamental provocation is. Sweeney famously last made headlines with the “Sydney Sweeney has great jeans” ad for American Eagle Outfitters. It was taken by many to be a call back to Donald Trump’s “You have great genes, you know that?” speech, which itself was taken as a densely layered challenge to the world, that his supporters were better human specimens than everyone else. Was the speech white supremacist or simply Trumpian-supremacist? You couldn’t really stick anything on him because, as ever, it was only atmospherically decipherable. Sweeney, however – with her very blondness, her unarguable whiteness – people did stick a white-supremacist agenda on, one she soon decried, saying she was against “divisiveness”.

Ever since, Sweeney has been taken as an anti-woke poster-girl, though since nobody can agree what “woke” means, still less what “anti-” it entails, this poster is more confusing than an avant garde typographer’s ball. She seems to want to kick that hornet’s nest with this Novig ad, but is it by inviting her own objectification? Or is there a complicated message in there about femaleness in elite sport, which has become such a lightning rod for anti-trans activism? Or are we supposed to disapprove of the pornification of the visual realm?

None of the above! Ariarne Titmus, four-time Olympic gold medal-winning swimmer, explained on Instagram: it’s “a kick in the face to every woman who had dedicated her life to perfecting her craft, but every woman who enjoys sports for what it really is – teamwork, friendship, dedication, excellence, unity”. And now she says it, yes, that makes perfect sense. What Sydney Sweeney’s game is, beyond almost-naked tennis, is anyone’s guess.

‘It’s about controlling your entire body’: how to start doing handstands

The Guardian Mon, 14 Sep 2026 16:00:10 GMT

Handstands display a mastery of one’s physical form that I have never quite felt – and they look cool. Experts share their advice for building up strength and practicing

My aspirations in life are modest: I want to write, spend time with my loved ones, and someday find a lipstick that flatters my skintone. But perhaps my greatest ambition is this: I want to be able to do a handstand.

Why? It turns the world upside down. It seems fun. It displays a mastery of one’s physical form that I have never quite felt. And it looks cool! Maybe it has to do with that one time in third grade when all my friends could do a handstand and I couldn’t, but that’s for me and my therapist to sort out later.

A handstand is an inversion, a type of position where one’s heart is above the head. Besides looking cool, there is a lot to gain from inversions. When the head is below the heart, oxygen-rich blood flow to the brain increases, according to the UC Irvine Integrative Health Institute. This helps “regulate neurotransmitters and nourish brain cells”. Other benefits include stress reduction and increased physical strength and mobility, says Antoinette Webb, a registered yoga teacher.

Below, experts share advice on how to start doing handstands.

“A handstand is a full-body inversion in which you support your weight through your hands while balancing upside down,” says Frank Medrano, a calisthenics athlete and coach.

Although it looks like an upper-body exercise, the position requires nearly every part of the body to work together, he says. The hands and forearms help maintain balance; the shoulders, upper back, chest and triceps support and stabilize the body; and the core, glutes and legs create the tension necessary to keep your body aligned.

“A strong handstand is not simply about kicking your hands overhead,” Medrano says. “It is about controlling your entire body as one connected unit.”

Because it is such an advanced exercise and it temporarily increases blood pressure in the head and upper body, there are certain groups who should be cautious or avoid handstands and other inversions, says Webb. These include individuals with conditions including high blood pressure; osteoporosis; neck, shoulder or spine injuries; and heart and eye conditions.

First, you need to figure out how strong your upper body is.

“I would start with downward dog, and hold that position for about 90 seconds,” says Dianne Bondy, a certified yoga teacher and pilates instructor, referring to the popular yoga position in which the body forms an inverted V, with hips in the air and hands and feet on the ground.

In order to prepare the rest of your body and help with mobility, Webb suggests working on yoga poses that help strengthen the core and hips, such as plank, locust, boat and cobra.

Once your upper body strength is sufficient, Bondy suggests progressing to positions where your feet are against a wall. This helps familiarize you with “the feeling of going upside down and pressing weight into your hands”, she explains.

Webb suggests building up comfort by learning to hold an L-shape against the wall, with your torso and legs at a right angle from each other, chest facing the wall. Your hands will be on the floor and your feet against the wall. How you get into this position is up to you – experiment safely to find your preferred method. This will help you learn how to tap into your breath and alignment, and practice bracing your body while pushing the ground away with your hands, she says.

As you progress, you can inch your feet gradually up the wall, says Medrano. The higher your feet go, the closer your hands, arms, torso and legs will move to the wall, until you are almost flush with it. Keep your body tight, and “only move as close as your strength and confidence allow”, he says. This process teaches body proper alignment without relying on the momentum of simply hoisting your legs into the air.

When you can hold a controlled wall stand, Medrano says you can try removing one foot from the wall at a time. Eventually, this may progress to removing both feet from the wall. Keep these attempts short. “Quality is more important than duration,” Medrano says.

When it comes to handstands, it’s not a matter of if you will fall, but when.

“You are absolutely going to fall, so how you can do so safely is the question you have to answer,” says Webb.

Medrano suggests “practicing stepping down deliberately”. One way to do this is learning how to turn out of the handstand, instead of falling over. This involves twisting from a handstand into a cartwheel, so that your legs swing to the side and you land on your feet. Make sure you have adequate space. (If that is difficult to envision, an instructional video, like this one, can help.)

More from How to start:

How to start meditating

How to start weightlifting

How to start budgeting

How to start running

“When I learned to do a handstand for the first time, I was in my 40s,” says Bondy. “I learned that it’s never too late. I still do them to this day.”

Bondy says she also learned that handstands were a “use it or lose it” skill. If you want to be able to keep doing it, you have to keep practicing.

Everyone’s progress will be different. If you’re miles away from doing a full handstand or wall stand, that’s fine.

“Comparing your journey to someone else’s is going to keep you struggling to take the first step,” says Webb. “Your handstand or headstand on the wall, with blocks or supported by another person is just as valid as someone in the middle of the floor standing on one hand.”

As with any physical goal, “give yourself grace and the space to see what you’re capable of,” says Webb.

How did the Guardian cover Oasis at Knebworth 1996? Well … we didn’t

The Guardian Mon, 14 Sep 2026 15:39:21 GMT

Noel Gallagher told fans ‘this is history’ but the paper opted to review support act the Charlatans instead, as that band returned from tragedy

News: Oasis announce 2027 tour, including return to Knebworth 30 years after historic concerts

Over two days in August 1996, Oasis played to 250,000 people at Knebworth House in Hertfordshire. Riding high on two bestselling albums, the concerts were seen as the crowning moment in their career.

The Guardian covered the weekend but Caroline Sullivan’s review concentrated on the Charlatans, one of the support acts. There was a picture of the Knebworth crowds on page 7, but the main review that day was of folk-rock band Fairport Convention’s Cropredy festival. There was also a review of the “anti-Oasis” Divine Comedy.

In fairness, the paper had recently carried a piece about Oasis’s Loch Lomond gigs, and it continued to report all the latest news about the band including the constant falling out/making up of the Gallagher brothers, and a Smurfs’ cover of Wonderwall. Read both pieces here:

By Caroline Sullivan 13 August 1996

“This is history,” Noel Gallagher shouted on Sunday, all vestiges of Mancunian cool gone as he surveyed the 125,000 disciples jamming Knebworth’s green acres to the horizon. Despite his fondness for overstatement, he was right. Oasis’s weekend shows were the largest outdoor gigs ever staged in Britain by one band. And if that wasn’t enough, the Morning Glory album was last week certified 10 times platinum (3m copies under UK classification), making it the UK’s seventh-bestselling album ever.

Today, as Noel and Our Kid ponder how to top it (Their own sitcom? A pub tour?), a handful of other bands will be nursing their own Knebworth memories. The Prodigy, Manic Street Preachers and Cast, though capable of headlining decent-sized venues themselves, became support acts for a day and were greeted with the mild enthusiasm reserved for introductory bands.

Only one outfit distracted the crowd’s attention from its noodles and beer, but for all the wrong reasons. “This is going to be a fairly difficult gig,” said Radio 1’s Jo Whiley, introducing the Charlatans. That they were playing at all, after the death of keyboardist Rob Collins in a car crash three weeks ago, elicited the biggest cheer of the day. Collins was responsible for the band’s trademark hypno-swirl sound, and his loss must put their future in doubt. However, they made a statement of sorts by honouring their Knebworth commitment, with Primal Scream’s keyboardist, Martin Duffy, standing in.

Aptly, it began to rain as they entered, a seagull soundtrack matching the mood. The drizzle stopped, but the sombreness remained, becoming a listlessness that dragged at the usually uplifting music (in which Collins’s Hammond flourishes were reproduced to the letter). Singer Tim Burgess, normally lost in a psychedelic trance, was blank-faced somewhere inside a hooded anorak. “New tune,” he murmured occasionally, as if feeling obliged to say something. After a while, they just seemed to stop. A sad, dispirited set, but one that deserves praise for having been done at all.

By Brian Logan 5 August 1996

Amble down Balloch’s main road any other day of the year and you’d be seduced – or bored – by its simplicity. You might stop at Corries tea shop for a cuppa and a scone; you might tinker with tartans in Loch Lomond Kilts. It’s a far cry from … well, from Manchester.

When locals heard that Oasis were to visit loch’n’roll upon them, they kicked up something of a fuss. How could sleepy Balloch take the strain of these rock gods and 80,000 boisterous disciples? We have, they protested, only one public lavatory.

Yet the horde that flocked to Loch Lomond this weekend was extended a warm(ish) reception. “West Dunbartonshire Council Welcomes You” read the signs; West Dunbartonshire residents, meanwhile, glared proprietorially from their windows.

Their concern was misplaced. If the Gallagher brothers are sharing next week’s bill at Knebworth with the Chemical Brothers, this week they had chemical toilets for company. Hundreds, erected defiantly at the very entrance so passing Highlanders would see that the mighty Oasis could do without their measly lavatory, thank you very much.

Rumour has it that forward-thinking revellers had come to Balloch Castle Country Park before the construction of the arena to bury their drugs beyond the investigation of the wiliest police officer. If there is an epidemic of blissed-out rabbits in the west of Scotland, we’ll know why. Continue reading

The video assistant referee officials who allowed Erling Haaland’s winning goal in the Manchester derby on Sunday have been stood down. Matt Donohue and his assistant, Blake Antrobus, have been told by Pro Ref they have not received appointments for this weekend’s round of Premier League fixtures.

Howard Webb, the chief ­refereeing officer, took the decision with his management team after a review of the weekend’s action. Their availa­bility will be reconsidered after the international break.

Donohue was called on to check Michael Oliver’s decision to ­disallow Haaland’s 60th-minute goal for offside. Using semi-automated ­offside technology, Donohue was able to establish that the Manchester City striker was onside and he overturned ­Oliver’s call. But he failed to spot Enzo Fernández had ­influenced play from an offside position, an ­infringement which Pro Ref said should have led him to recommend an on-field review.

This is the first time officials have been made to stand down this season owing to an error. Donohue, an EFL referee since 2018, has taken charge of three Championship matches this season as well as his VAR work. His EFL profile says he has completed Pro Ref’s “Enhanced VAR ­Training Programme”. ­Antrobus is also an assistant referee in the ­Premier League and ran the line in the first three matchdays.

Phones are the new cigarettes: why restaurants are discouraging and even banning them

The Guardian Mon, 14 Sep 2026 15:31:59 GMT

Would you hand in your phone at the door in exchange for a free bottle of wine? One restaurateur has tried that – and there are now many other gambits that are encouraging us to connect

Name: Phone bans.

Age: Their provenance is considerable; their time is now.

Appearance: Groups of people eating together, talking together and laughing together, while also twitching slightly from withdrawal.

So this is specifically to do with banning phones in restaurants? Restaurants and bars, yes.

Hardly a new thing, is it? No. Ironically, a decade ago many fine dining establishments were unbanning mobiles, surrendering to the idea that people couldn’t be stopped from posting photographs of their food.

I suppose it was considered good for business. Not any more – at the Spy Bar in London, they put a sticker over your phone’s camera lens at the door.

What’s the point? People can just peel the sticker off. It’s supposed to work on a psychological level – to preserve privacy and allow people to enjoy themselves without distraction.

Shouldn’t a ban be more, erm, enforceable? They certainly can be. At Antagonist, a bar in Charlotte, North Carolina, customers are required to put their phones in a locked pouch of the type used to enforce phone bans in schools. At the Trophy Room in Phoenix, Arizona, guests’ phones are stored in a vintage filing cabinet during their visit.

Sounds like prison. At the Clink restaurant in London they lock all phones in an outside cabin, but that’s because the restaurant is actually inside HMP Brixton, where possession of a mobile phone is prohibited.

OK, maybe a phone ban should be less enforceable than that. Some places use a carrot instead of a stick. At Al Condominio in Verona, Italy, customers are offered a free bottle of wine if they surrender their phones before the meal.

Does that work? Apparently 90% of customers accept the challenge.

As would I for free wine. Other restaurants simply have a no phones policy, in a bid to encourage conversation and to re-establish focus on the food and the experience.

And the clientele are in favour? For the most part. “I strongly encourage people to give it a chance, and sometimes they don’t and they go somewhere else,” Antagonist’s general manager told the Wall Street Journal.

Still, it sounds as if it’s becoming more widespread. Big chains are now beginning to crack down. Pizza Express initiated phone-free afternoons last summer, and even Wetherspoons has drawn a line.

There’s no way I would go into a Wetherspoons without my phone. No worries – they just want you to keep it on silent.

Do say: “Take my phone, please. Anything that encourages human connection is worth sacrificing a few hours of doomscrolling for.”

Don’t say: “I can still do my podcast from here though, right?”
