Hunt and Kerr have lit up summer, but will star athletes make Spoty shortlist?

The Guardian Mon, 14 Sep 2026 15:30:39 GMT

‘It’s not a given, that’s the reality,’ Kerr says in Budapest

Athletes cautious over BBC’s informal shortlist policy

It should be the biggest no-brainer of the sporting year. After a summer where athletics has captured hearts and headlines, and made so many fans fall back in love with it again, either Amy Hunt or Josh Kerr should win the award for BBC Sports Personality of the Year.

The bookies’ odds suggest many others think the same way: Hunt is the even-money favourite, Kerr is second, with Harry Kane a stride or two back in third. Yet Kerr knows he cannot take anything for granted.

In 2023 the 28-year-old Scot won the world 1500m title in a clash for the ages against Jakob Ingebrigtsen. But then he fell foul of the BBC’s curious reluctance to pick two athletes from the same sport in its six-person shortlist. Instead the wheelchair tennis player Alfie Hewett, and Rory McIlroy, who won four of his five Ryder Cup matches that year, got the nod ahead of him.

“Spoty is massively important,” Kerr said after winning the Ultimate Championship in Budapest. “Everyone grew up watching it. It’s a massive award, and I would be truly honoured to be on that shortlist up against some of the best athletes of all time this year. I would love to go, but it’s not a given, that’s the reality.”

Kerr is right to be cautious given that only twice since 2017 has the BBC veered off its informal policy. The first came in 2019 when the athletes Dina Asher-Smith and Katarina Johnson-Thompson were selected. Then it happened again when the footballers Hannah Hampton and Chloe Kelly got the nod.

However, on both occasions, those selections helped to balance the male-female split. But in a year where Kane could win the Ballon D’Or, Matt Weston has won two Winter Olympic medals, Luke Littler has dominated darts, and McIlroy won the Masters again, it is not a given the BBC will necessarily go for both track and field stars.

Kerr’s claims are surely stronger than anyone given he obliterated a world mile record that had stood for 27 years, and backed it up by winning the world indoor, Commonwealth Games and Ultimate Championship.

Late on Sunday night he accepted that amounted to pretty much the perfect season. “Outside of an Olympic year, I can’t give any more than that,” he said. “I’m a clean athlete doing it the right way, trying to show the way that I’m doing it. And you know, that’s all I can give. This, genuinely, has been the best year of my career.”

Next year he wants to go for the world 1500m record, but he stressed it would not be easy. “People don’t know what that toll is on your body,” he said. “It feels like getting hit by a bus the next day.” Kerr also wants Hunt on the shortlist. “She’s had a fantastic season,” he said. “She deserves to be there.”

Last month Hunt became the first person in the 96-year history of the European Athletics Championships to win four gold medals. Few athletes have a bigger personality as she showed again at the weekend by speaking out against Sydney Sweeney sexualising sport, and about the difficulties of performing when on her period.

Canada should become an EU state in all but name. Here’s how to make that a reality

The Guardian Mon, 14 Sep 2026 15:19:03 GMT

From the UK to Japan, so many countries need to quickly be brought inside the European tent without the rigours of full membership

The worst conclusion to draw from Iceland’s EU referendum result last month would be that the country, apparently now on Donald Trump’s imperial map along with Canada and Greenland, wanted to distance itself from Europe. Rather, the decision to refuse the reopening of EU accession talks shows that asking voters to choose between membership of the 27-nation bloc and staying outside the club is too binary. Some countries want to be inside the European tent without necessarily becoming members. The EU needs a new status for them.

There are existing models of close cooperation. Iceland and Norway, for example, participate in much of the single market through the European Economic Area (EEA). A range of other partial, gradual or associated membership options for candidate countries is being debated.

What I am proposing is different from any of them. It is not about setting up a stepping stone to accession, nor is it primarily about access to the single market. Instead, it is about letting like-minded countries combine with the EU when geopolitical and geo-economic necessities demand it, without them having to sign up to a predetermined constitutional outcome.

The main criterion for the novel status I call “integrated partnership” would be geopolitical rather than geographical. A country would not have to aspire to EU membership to qualify. It would not even have to be situated in Europe. Iceland, the UK and Norway are obvious potential candidates, but so are Canada, Japan and South Korea.

These countries would be inside the tent wherever legally and politically possible, pooling sovereignty across specific policy areas. This relationship could ultimately amount to quasi-membership, with corresponding rights and obligations. Unlike membership of the EEA, however, it would extend beyond the economy. Defence, security, economic security and foreign policy would be as fundamental to the relationship as trade and the single market.

Countries already seeking full EU membership, of which there are nine at the moment, will continue to prioritise that end goal. But the EU will struggle to deliver on its promises to all of those in the queue within a reasonable timeframe. Political resistance to the union’s expansion beyond the 27 existing members could intensify if key national elections next year create a shift in the EU’s majority political outlook. Already, internal reforms, budgetary concerns and the complexities of accession could leave some countries waiting for years.

All sides would benefit from giving these queueing nations another option. Ukraine or the western Balkan countries should not remain stranded in a geopolitical waiting room simply because the EU lacks the political will or administrative bandwidth to admit them. Of course, safeguards are essential: this kind of advanced partnership must be a bridge to membership for those seeking it, not a car park that allows governments of existing EU nations to renege on promises if they become electorally unpopular.

The defining test for partners must be genuine like-mindedness around democratic values: a sustained commitment to liberal democracy, the rule of law, political sovereignty and an international order based on rules.

Canada should be among the first candidates. The EU-Canada summit in October should go beyond another list of worthy deliverables and start the process of establishing a special status so deep that the country could eventually become the equivalent of an EU member state in all but name. Ursula von der Leyen should announce as much in her annual state of the union address this week. With Canada’s relationship with the US on the ropes, Brussels has an eager partner in Mark Carney, who said on Sunday that he wants a “unique alliance” with the EU.

But that would require clear commitments from Ottawa as well as Brussels. Integrated partners should not get a free ticket to the benefits of EU policies without corresponding obligations and costs.

The case for this is becoming easier to make. Democracies face increasingly aggressive behaviour from authoritarian powers. Middle powers risk being isolated, divided and picked off individually. As Carney has argued, they must act together in response to the rupture of the old international order. Integrated partnership could help operationalise Carney’s argument.

There is also a more uncomfortable reason for new geopolitical architecture. It cannot be assumed that countries, even those supposedly joined at the hip through the EU, will always continue on a like-minded path. France or Germany could in the future be governed by illiberal anti-European forces unwilling to defend the principles on which European integration rests.

Sign up to This is Europe

The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment

after newsletter promotion

A network encompassing democratic EU members and their close partners could then become a political counterweight, helping to preserve collective action when consensus inside the EU becomes impossible. This should not become an alternative EU. But Europe cannot base its geopolitical strategy on the assumption that every one of its governments will remain committed to European integration or even liberal democracy.

The European project emerged from the ruins of the second world war. Now, in a very different geopolitical context, we need ambitious mechanisms for bringing like-minded democracies together. But full EU membership cannot be the only route to deep integration. Maximum integration without a predetermined end point should now become the objective.

Iceland’s vote, driven by concerns over fisheries and other totemic national issues, shows why new thinking and geopolitical ambition are needed. Geography should no more determine who can be inside Europe’s tent than the time it takes to conduct painstaking enlargement negotiations. Increasingly, the decisive question is whether Europe can club together with all countries that are prepared to defend democratic principles together.

Fabian Zuleeg is chief executive and chief economist at the European Policy Centre

Oasis announce 2027 tour, including return to Knebworth 30 years after historic concerts

The Guardian Mon, 14 Sep 2026 15:00:22 GMT

After 2025’s wildly lucrative reunion, the Gallagher brothers will tour the UK, Ireland and US, and revisit the Hertfordshire site of their greatest live triumph

From the archive: How did the Guardian cover Oasis at Knebworth 1996? Well … we didn’t

Oasis have finally confirmed new tour dates for 2027, including their long-rumoured return to Knebworth for a run of shows 30 years after they played a historic two nights at the Hertfordshire venue in 1996.

“Start the celebrations!”, the band said in a statement. “After a period of reflection, The Most Damaging Pop Cultural Force in Recent British History” – a quote from a Guardian opinion piece about the band – “has declared itself fit for purpose and will once again return to lift the spirits of the people. Come witness the fitness. It shall be a sight to behold.”

Titled Oasis Live 27, the dates encompass the UK, Ireland, mainland Europe and the US, beginning in Glasgow on 21 May, and touring through Manchester, Munich, Barcelona, Amsterdam, Paris, Rome, Boston, Las Vegas and Slane Castle (north of Dublin), ending with four nights at Knebworth in September.

The band had teased the news in a massive drone display above Manchester’s Etihad stadium last week, after hinting at the dates on Instagram.

The tour follows Oasis’s acclaimed 2025 reunion, which saw them play 41 dates spanning the UK, Europe, North and South America, east Asia and Australia, 16 years after they split in 2009. “You struggle to think of another artist that’s received such a vociferous reception,” wrote Guardian critic Alexis Petridis in a five-star review of the first night of the tour in Cardiff.

The 2027 tour will be Oasis’s first visit to mainland Europe since their reunion and adds US cities they didn’t visit during that run. Their return to Paris will be particularly poignant, given it was shortly before a 2009 set at the city’s Rock en Seine festival that the band first split up.

In the UK, tickets will cost between £71.50 and £266.60. Those hoping to buy them will have a happier experience than those in the same position last year: all pricing information for Oasis Live 27 has been shared in advance after action by the competition watchdog forced Ticketmaster to change how it advertises tickets, including ending “misleading” information about seats, after fan backlash over its handling of the 2025 tour.

Last year, the use of “tiered” pricing meant that some fans, expecting to pay £148.50 per ticket, found themselves faced with costs of £350 at the checkout – and only a matter of minutes in which to decide whether to go ahead with their purchases. Now, Ticketmaster must tell fans 24 hours in advance if tiered pricing will be used, which tickets it covers and how the system works. When the sale is live, the price range must be shared and updated as tickets sell out.

Anyone wanting a ticket for 2027’s tour must register between now and 4pm BST on 17 September. The registration has been introduced “to reduce queuing times and organised ticket touting in order to give genuine fans the best possible chance to buy tickets,” according to organisers.

Fans had a chance to revisit the 2025 tour – or catch up on what they missed – as a documentary about the reunion, Don’t Look Back in Anger, hit cinemas last week after premiering at the Venice film festival. It earned glowing reviews for its emotional portrait of the band’s fans.

The documentary didn’t touch on the furore around ticket prices, other than one onstage comment from Liam Gallagher: after referring to the people in the cheap seats, he added: “Actually there are no cheap seats, sorry about that.”

The news that Oasis would return to Knebworth was first teased by an unlikely suspect, the British peer Baroness Taylor of Stevenage. In October 2025, she suggested in the House of Lords that Oasis would be playing five shows “in the fantastic venue of Knebworth House”, just a mile away from her own residence.

She quickly retracted her comments in the chamber, clarifying to the Guardian that she was “speaking hypothetically following speculation that they would play Knebworth again as they did in August 1996”.

In August, it was reported that SJM Concerts managing director Simon Moran had secured an events licence for Knebworth, prompting further speculation about an Oasis appearance. The licence would cover audiences of 125,000 people.

At the original 1996 dates, the band played to 250,000 fans – just one tenth of the number who applied for tickets, estimated at the time to be more than 4% of the entire British population. “This is history,” Noel Gallagher told the Knebworth crowd on the second night. The band recently started selling replicas of Noel and Liam’s respective outfits on the night.

A 2021 documentary, the prosaically titled Oasis Knebworth 1996, positioned the concerts as “the peak of British culture” wrote Guardian music editor Ben Beaumont-Thomas in a four-star review. The film’s voiceovers, he continued, implied that “all live music went downhill afterwards. It’s a lie every generation tells itself.” Liam subsequently headlined the park in June 2022.

UK Music estimated that the band’s five nights at Manchester’s Heaton Park last year led to music tourist spending in the north-west rising 16% year on year to £1.4bn. Momentum behind the tour was also credited with boosting the UK’s ongoing vinyl revival.

Oasis are also rumoured to be headlining Glastonbury 2027, the festival’s return after a fallow year in 2026.

Their reunion poured more fuel on the fire of enduring Britpop nostalgia, sparking a critically panned play documenting the rivalry between Oasis and Blur, an album called Britpop by Robbie Williams and even an embrace of Oasis in the US, a country that had been historically immune to their charms.

Ancestors review – messy but moving ghostly drama about the Aids crisis

The Guardian Mon, 14 Sep 2026 14:58:22 GMT

Toronto film festival: Saipan standout Éanna Hardwicke is a soulful gay man looking for a missing friend in a striking yet muddled debut

It’s not normal to regularly contemplate mortality in your twenties, to ask questions about where we might go after we die and whether any part of our legacy will even matter in the years following. But for gay men in the 1980s, death was everywhere.

In David Turpin’s intermittently impactful debut Ancestors, the director tries to make a connection with those men who lived through the very worst years of the Aids crisis. Turpin, born in 1982, might not have the first-hand experience but he bears the scars passed on from generation to generation and like many young gay men coming of age in the years after, likely experienced a watered down version of the shame and fear those before him once felt.

His film is about how bridges are built between past and future, living and dead, old and young, and how those who have been pushed out of society work about trying to create and sustain their own. Set in a foggy, ghostly London in 1988, Turpin’s dreamy and mysterious film is trying to cast a spell (he has referred to it as a “séance” in interviews) and it’s one that works incredibly well at times and wears off far too easily at others. As with many a first movie, there’s a lot thrown at the wall here with scrappy ambition prioritised over laser focus and while that’s admirable, it can also be a little frustrating.

What’s most consistent is a mesmerising performance from Éanna Hardwicke, the Irish actor who was also one of the best things about last year’s Toronto film festival, playing Roy Keane in underseen World Cup workplace drama Saipan. Again he brings real, combustible angst to the role but here it’s of a far different kind, aimed at the rapidly disintegrating world around him and the one person he wants to save from disintegrating with it. He plays Beau, a gay man working in a caff owned by “Auntie” Maurice (Rupert Everett), an old queen who collects both framed pictures of the female actors he idolises as well as young strays. The latest of whom is Tiny (Jack Wolfe), a 20-year-old in need of work. When Beau later sees him cruising in the park and finds out he has nowhere to stay, he brings him back to stay in an apartment shared with his best friend, Shell (a luminous Jessica Reynolds).

Refreshingly there’s no sexual tension between the pair (Beau says early on that Tiny isn’t his type) and instead they become friends, a far more compelling and under-explored gay male dynamic. Like Maurice did with him, Beau also feels a sense of responsibility for Tiny, an overwhelming weight at such a grim time and after Tiny reveals that he is positive, the objective changes from keeping him safe to keeping him alive. The film jumps back and forth in time, and to other places, as Tiny goes missing and Beau must try to find him. Early on Beau tries to get Tiny to read his collection of Jean Genet novels but he tells him that he isn’t interested in tales of detectives and instead prefers “love stories and ghost stories”. Turpin also has little interest in the fact-finding grind of actually tracking someone down and more about the love between the pair and the ghosts that surround them.

For a film that plays with reality, dreams, nightmares, the past, the future and the afterlife and slips between timelines and from colour to black and white, it often works best in its more grounded conversational scenes. His direction might get overly precious but Turpin’s dialogue is natural and direct and we never doubt Hardwicke’s authenticity. The film around him can meander a little, in its worst moments feeling like a short that’s been expanded beyond its means, and while some of the atmosphere is entirely enveloping, sometimes the visuals can be a little ropey. There are misfiring gambits like a transfixing but inconsequential Christina Hendricks as a golden age actor who comes to life and a few too many underwhelming musical interludes at a local gay bar (save for one wrenching cover of Tim Buckley’s Song to the Siren which is wisely played again at the end). I was moved by so much – a picture of Tiny added to an expanding wall filled with other gay men who got sick, Beau’s anxiousness over whether he might also have it and how intimate he should then be with Shell or Maurice, how Beau grapples with the idea of hopelessness without despair – but then alienated by so many others.

The last act hinges on a more conventional reveal that feels a little at odds with the stranger, fuzzier movie that Turpin seems more focused on making. It doesn’t quite have the gut-punch impact it should, a more conceptually interesting idea than an emotionally effective one, but the very last scene does bring us back under that spell. In its swirl of emotions, ideas and styles, Ancestors can get a little lost in the mist but when, in its finest moments, it all clears, there’s something haunting in front of us.

Experts quit Lucy Letby’s defence team over ‘scientific credibility’ concerns

The Guardian Mon, 14 Sep 2026 14:47:19 GMT

Some of the arguments inconsistent with ‘available evidence, science and established physiology’, say pair

Two leading experts have withdrawn from Lucy Letby’s defence team over concerns about the “scientific credibility” of some of its evidence.

The former neonatal nurse is challenging her convictions for murdering seven babies and attempting to murder seven others at the Countess of Chester hospital in north-west England.

The Criminal Cases Review Commission (CCRC), the UK’s miscarriage of justice watchdog, is considering a dossier of evidence submitted last year by experts on her behalf.

Two experts withdrew from Letby’s defence team on Monday. They said that although they stood by their assessment that it was “very unlikely” two of the babies were poisoned, some of the arguments being put forward on her behalf were “inconsistent with the available evidence, science and established physiology”.

Helen Shannon, a British chemical engineering expert, and Geoff Chase, a professor of bioengineering based in New Zealand, produced a 100-page report last year casting doubt on her convictions for poisoning two babies with insulin.

They told the Guardian last year there was a “very strong level of reasonable doubt” about those two convictions, which formed a central part of the prosecution case against Letby. The 36-year-old nurse was convicted in 2023 of trying to murder two newborn boys, known as Baby 6 and Baby 12, by spiking their feeding bags with insulin.

Letby is serving 15 whole-life orders after she was convicted across two trials at Manchester crown court of murdering seven babies and attempting to murder seven others, with two attempts on one of her victims, between June 2015 and June 2016.

Shannon and Chase said on Monday they stood by their assessment, but could not support other evidence used by Letby’s defence team relating to the insulin cases.

In a letter to the CCRC, the experts said: “Whilst it is entirely legitimate for the defence to advance multiple arguments, some of the other arguments now being put forward we cannot support as scientifically credible and which have, in our view, fundamental unresolvable problems.”

They said the strategy of Letby’s defence team, led by her barrister Mark McDonald, was “placing the long-term interests of Ms Letby at serious, unnecessary and unacceptable risk” and that those “consequences also extend to the families” of the babies who died and were injured.

They added: “We cannot, with integrity, support arguments which are inconsistent with the available evidence, science and established physiology … After disclosing these concerns, continued association with arguments we believe are demonstrably inaccurate creates a serious ethical issue under the professional engineering codes governing us in New Zealand and the UK, and exposes us to professional sanction.”

McDonald, Letby’s barrister, said: “We now have evidence from a number of leading international experts in insulin, endocrinology and laboratory medicine which fundamentally undermines the scientific evidence relied upon at trial. Importantly, the case does not stand or fall on any one expert.

“The strength of the new evidence lies in its breadth and convergence, with independent experts from different disciplines and jurisdictions identifying fundamental problems with the scientific basis upon which the jury were invited to conclude that babies [6] and [12] had been deliberately poisoned.”

The CCRC, which has been reviewing the convictions for 18 months, declined to comment.

A public inquiry into the murders will publish its findings on Tuesday. The review, led by Lady Justice Kathryn Thirlwall, is expected to highlight a number of missed opportunities for bosses to intervene after doctors raised the alarm about a spate of unexplained deaths on the neonatal unit in 2015 and 2016.

A criminal investigation is ongoing into potential corporate manslaughter and gross negligence manslaughter at the Countess of Chester hospital.

Sydney Sweeney’s prediction ad is cynical, unhealthy and reveals plenty about modern sports

The Guardian Mon, 14 Sep 2026 14:30:26 GMT

The actor’s latest promotion has stirred outrage but will no doubt be good for the prediction markets hoping to lure in young men

Prediction markets are a cynical business.

Many customers will lose money, and the real product may just be the delightful dopamine hit that comes in that brief window between placing a bet and its outcome – which is statistically more likely to be a disappointment than a victory. So the bettor has to think they are buying more than their own fleecing.

Enter Sydney Sweeney, the icily beautiful actor who stars in a sports prediction market company’s ad campaign wearing little more than a bat and balls. She’s not a professional athlete, but she functions to remind us that plenty of people want us to believe the best woman in sports is the one who appeals to men.

It’s the same ethos that puts capturing the male gaze on a list of hiring criteria for TV sideline reporters, and made Olivia Dunne the richest athlete in college sports. But of course Dunne put in years of training as an elite gymnast, and didn’t serve to make a mockery of women’s sports.

Does Sweeney? After her American Eagle campaign was criticized as eugenics-adjacent, she eventually issued vague comments about how, yawn, surprised she was at the outcry. If she were actually bothered, she might check the optics of campaigns like the one causing so much outcry at the moment. Certainly once she saw how her blond, blue-eyed image was being utilized and perceived, she would be more discerning when sifting through the endorsement opportunities that came her way.

Her lack of apparent concern must be as well-compensated as her one-note acting. The prediction company she is promoting in this campaign lists her as a strategic partner and equity holder and, if the company can negotiate shifting legal terrain, that could make Sweeney orders of magnitude richer for absorbing the critique.

Olympic swimmer and four-time gold medalist Ariarne Titmus is one of many professional athletes who have expressed disappointment and anger with the provocatively regressive campaign.

“How do we live in a world where monetising a women’s body and sexualising women’s sport is still a thing?” she wrote on Instagram.

Women’s sports are being professionalized at a pace eclipsing anything we’ve previously seen. Leagues are expanding, ratings and attendance are up, and some teams have been valued at more than $500m. Female athletes have real power – financially and with their social media platforms. Any company looking to get into the space has a pick of champions who would communicate the company’s message.

But for all that progress, there are executives and fans who would prefer that sports looked how they did back when they were kids. Many of them are gatekeepers in traditional media, and many outlets still treat women’s sports less seriously than men’s. Purdue academic Cheryl Cooky’s new research details the trend in all its glory.

In an era in which stoking outrage can win elections and make you a wealthy sports bloviator, there are fewer actual consequences to stop a company from trying to offend potential consumers.

Of course, it is still possible to create a marketing campaign so disastrous it can severely damage a company. Look no further than the golf content specialist Good Good, which recently ran and then retracted a commercial which appeared to make light of violence against women.

Good Good’s front office has been shaken up. But the company lost a partnership with industry stalwart Callaway Golf, a reality show it launched was cancelled, stores pulled merchandise off the shelves, and its name was pulled off a PGA Tour tournament. Co-founder Garrett Clark eventually posted an eight-minute apology video, but whenever you have to announce that you don’t condone domestic violence, you’ve lost control of the narrative. Maybe golf isn’t the best place to go for edgy.

Prediction markets, however, are in a particularly calculating line of business. As was the case with cigarette companies before them, few people believe the product is actually good for anyone. There are allegations that people with inside information on war and troop movements are placing bets in the liminal space between planning and action.

So what is there for a prediction market to lose by stoking outrage with a proven outrage-stoker like Sweeney? Unlike with Good Good, there is no established brand partner to disappoint. The sports prediction consumers that the maker of the Sweeney ad is likely courting are the same young men who will be titillated by the actor and delighted by the subversive naughtiness of all the froth.

The message cynically fits the audience.

Even though prediction markets aren’t the same as traditional sportsbooks, they are in the same general family. Sports consumers can’t escape the ads, the conversations, the sponsorships when watching a game. It seems everyone wants a piece of the action.

What those behind the Sweeney ad are actually predicting is a column like this, and the outrage of athletes who are trying to push back the regressive tide. I’d wager they hope to use it to attract more young men to open accounts. After all, poison in the discourse is good for business.

‘The eye-gouging was very, very satisfying’: how we made cave horror classic The Descent

The Guardian Mon, 14 Sep 2026 14:23:56 GMT

‘The child crawler whose head I crush with my boot was only 11, bless him. It was actually me stamping on a cauliflower’

I was introduced to Christian Colson at Celador Films off the back of [2002 horror film] Dog Soldiers, and I pitched them a project – actually a feature-length version of my student graduation film – about zombies on an oil rig. They liked it but said it was too expensive, so on the train back to Newcastle I was asking myself what would make a really scary horror film that could be contained and so made on a budget. I was thinking of things set in the dark and was like, well … caves. At the back of my mind was a school trip to a lead mine where the guide had said, “OK, everybody, turn your lights off” and, for the first time, I experienced a darkness that I just couldn’t fathom.

We wanted the film to feel as realistic as possible: when you’re caving, the only lights you have are what you take with you. There are no beautiful shafts of light making everything look pretty. It meant having huge portions of the screen in total darkness, so only when a character turns around and shines a light you finally see what’s in the shadows.

Darkness was definitely my friend, but it did mean a lot of planning because each character had to have something they could light the scene with, even if it was just a box of matches. Sam McCurdy, the director of photography, and I discussed lighting sources that we could potentially use, and I structured the film around who had which light at which time. This gave us a lighting scheme: if you’re with the fire, it’s Sarah. If it’s a torch, it’s Juno.

There isn’t a single real cave in the whole film. It was a mixture of amazing sets by Simon Bowles, a couple of matte paintings and a miniature set built by Leigh Took – the water pouring down the waterfall wasn’t water, it’s salt.

For the crawlers, I wanted something very basic-looking, not too many lines or details. The challenge was how to make them scary but keep them human, because the notion is that these are the cavemen who stayed in the cave rather than those who left the dark and started building cabins in the open. Visually they were a hybrid of Nosferatu and Iggy Pop, but movement-wise I thought we should make them like spiders – the way they’ll stop and be perfectly still before suddenly going off at 100 miles an hour and then stopping again.

I conceptualised the film as Sarah’s descent into being this primal savage: her undergoing a rebirth in order to survive, even though you’re not sure she’s going to be able to go back to society afterwards.

This was the era of FHM, Loaded and all those lads’ mags, so I initially thought it was going to be girls looking sexy in tight spaces covered in blood and gunge. I wasn’t interested in that. When I read the script, though, it was excellent. It was about a grieving mother and I also needed to be physically strong and brave. I thought, “I have to do this part because I don’t know if I’ll be able to pull it off.”

We weren’t allowed to see the crawlers or even any pictures of them. I was the first to see one because we were shooting chronologically once we got into the caves. The others were all asking “what does it look like?!” but I didn’t really know because it was quite far away. I just knew it was grey or white and slimy, and it looked a bit like Gollum.

I think Neil was right to keep us apart, because when we were faced with them, I was being leapt at by a really scary man, basically naked, who’d been training for months and months – that really focuses the mind. When we came to fight them, they were so animalistic it was really unnerving. The actors had figured out how the crawlers’ system worked and their different characteristics. You felt like you were fighting a pack with all its dynamics, and that was pretty intimidating.

That whole sequence where Sarah goes into survival mode was great. First I had the dying scene with Alex Reid, who played Beth, just making it look really easy. It was like, “OK, Alex, you’ve had an ice pick through your neck, but it’s really important that you tell these plot points …” And she was, “Yeah, cool, no problem.” And then, of course, I cave her head in with a stone. Then I get leapt on by a child crawler. He was only like 11, bless him, and I crushed his head with my boot, which was actually me stamping on a cauliflower. Then the mother finds out, and we have this fight sequence where one mother has to kill another to survive. The eye-gouging was very, very satisfying. Then another crawler comes along and I bash his head in too. Afterwards I’m submerged in this pool of blood, which was a Jacuzzi that they’d overflowed. This amazing stunt girl had to do the run and jump, because the pool was so shallow they couldn’t insure an actor to do it. All I had to do was emerge and take the glory.

In the press, it was all about “girl power”. But we were like: “Have you seen what we do to each other?!” What was very girl power was how fiercely we actors supported each other and we continue to do that. The only way you can really show love is by turning up for your friends, and the six of us have done that repeatedly for the last 21 years or so. We’ve got a WhatsApp group and still meet regularly. I do wonder, if we’d met on a different project, would the same thing happen? Or was it the film? If you throw a group of people in a cave, maybe you all come out bonded for life.

The Descent is available on 4K UHD

The latest inquest into failure by an American team on European soil involves slow greens, the perception of a premature celebration and a curious absence of statistical backup. Angela Stanford, whose Solheim Cup team were defeated by Europe in the Netherlands on Sunday, warned Jim Furyk’s Ryder Cup contingent to take note.

Stanford used the numbers-based evidence of Justin Ray to assist with decision-making and Furyk will do likewise at Adare Manor next year. In the aftermath of the 15-13 defeat and assessing Ray’s input, Stanford clearly had an underlying gripe. “I’m wondering how honest to be,” she said.

“Justin Ray is extremely helpful. We were missing some pieces this week. Like, in Spain [in 2023] we had people giving us strokes gained in each match, even in practice. And we didn’t have that this year.

“Because I know he’s working with Jim in the Ryder Cup, just now in the locker room, I told him exactly what he needed to do for Jim. Those things do matter and Justin was a huge help. He got us to this point.

“It’s easy to get blown out over here. So I think we had the right formula and he helped us make that formula, so Justin Ray is awesome.”

Pressed on why there was not the adequate backup resource she had referenced, Stanford said: “We just didn’t. See, that’s why I couldn’t be so honest with you.”

It should be remembered that the teams were level, at 8-8, before a Sunday singles session where the USA team stood as the favourites. Following Stanford’s logic, she appears to be implying her team were denied the opportunity to take a lead into day three.

Saturday’s conclusion had felt significant. Extraordinary pieces of play by Jennifer Kupcho on the last two holes meant she and Lindy Duncan claimed an unlikely point against Carlota Ciganda and Céline Boutier. Social media lit up with video of the USA team celebrating with beers on the bus back to their hotel. “They drink on Saturday, we drink on Sunday,” Europe’s team chanted when they made the same journey a day later.

Stanford disputed any sense of untimely euphoria. She had been unwilling to ask the American players to tone down their joy. “That’s kind of tricky because you don’t ever want to take away from that moment,” she said. “The worst thing I could have done is go in there and be like: ‘OK, y’all. Come off this high.’ You don’t want to take away from those moments. We’re never going to see anything like that again.

“I think they handled it very well. We’ve never seen that so we don’t really know how to react. I talked to Kupcho and everybody and they’re like, ‘Yeah, we got good rest, but it did take a minute to come off because it was a pretty high, high.’”

Another element was the putting surfaces. Anna Nordqvist, Europe’s captain, shrugged off any notion of gamesmanship by pointing out “we are in Europe in September”, but the pace of the greens had caught out the USA team.

Beck: Ride Lonesome review – stunning end to the heartache trilogy of Sea Change and Morning Phase

The Guardian Mon, 14 Sep 2026 13:00:58 GMT

(Iliad/Capitol)On his first album in seven years, Beck keeps the quality control extremely high as he surveys mid-50s malaise in the wake of divorce

The last time Beck released an album it was 2019 and the singer-songwriter found himself in a strange and unenviable position. In some quarters, the arrival of Hyperspace was eagerly anticipated precisely because his personal life was in turmoil. Nine months before its release, his 15-year marriage to actor Marissa Ribisi had ended in divorce, an experience he understandably described as heartbreaking. Unfortunately for him, there exists a pervasive argument that Beck’s greatest work is born out of misery.

His beloved 2002 album Sea Change featured a set of disconsolate acoustic songs written in the wake of a break-up with his long-term girlfriend Leigh Limon that Beck had initially thought were too personal for public consumption. They were certainly very different from the knowing, postmodern approach with which he’d made his name, but no matter: Sea Change went on to become a huge critical and commercial success. It wasn’t entirely clear what prompted the gloomy mood of 2014’s Morning Phase, but it very much seemed to be cut from similar musical and lyrical cloth. Some critics suggested it was the best album of his career; it subsequently won three Grammys, including album of the year. Given the circumstances, there was much pre-release speculation that Hyperspace would be a companion piece.

Instead, Hyperspace was synth-heavy, produced by Pharrell Williams and clearly influenced by vaporwave: its tone was dreamily buoyant and noticeably light on wracked soul-bearing. After its release, Beck seemed to tacitly suggest to fans of Sea Change and Morning Phase that there wouldn’t be any more where they came from. “When I try to shoe-horn my life into a song,” he told the New Yorker, “it gets really ham-fisted.”

Seven years on, he appears to have reconsidered. The first thing you hear on Ride Lonesome is a softly strummed acoustic guitar, echoey pedal steel and Beck’s voice. “Walk away, hang your head on the hollow moon,” he sings, as the album’s title track gets under way: should there be any lingering doubt about the mood it’s intent on evoking, it goes on to reference Julie London’s Cry Me a River and Johnny Thunders’ You Can’t Put Your Arms Around a Memory. “It feels like I’ve been here before,” he sings on Bleed, as strings gently rise and fall around him.

He certainly has. There’s an intentionality about the way Ride Lonesome reconvenes the team responsible for Sea Change and Morning Phase – the former’s producer Nigel Godrich is once more behind the mixing desk, the backing musicians who appear on both albums are present and correct, the orchestrations are the work of Beck’s father David Campbell – and about the artists the music here evokes. As on Sea Change’s Round the Bend and Morning Phase’s Heart Is a Drum, the ghosts of Nick Drake and his string arranger Robert Kirby are very clearly summoned up, most noticeably on In the Night. On Run Away, we find Beck exactly where he was on Sea Change’s The Golden Age and Morning Phase’s Unforgiven: alone, behind the wheel of a car in the small hours, aimlessly driving around in an attempt to assuage his unhappiness.

Similar sound, similar mood, similar lyrical themes: of course, the danger is of diminishing returns. But Ride Lonesome never feels like a pale imitation or a craven attempt to recapture past glories. That’s partly because of the standard of the songwriting. Beck has suggested that one reason the album took so long to make is because of stringent quality control: songs were recorded, then set aside for years, then reconsidered, a huge amount of material was discarded. You can tell: everything here, from the sparse country-rock of Slow Canyon to the lush, harmony-drenched Falling Through My Hands is melodically exquisite; every song has the requisite emotional impact.

But it’s also because Ride Lonesome is clearly an album made by a noticeably older artist than either of its predecessors: its mood is marked not just by the collapse of a relationship, but a sense of time passing, of things – to borrow a phrase from Nick Drake – moving just a little too fast. “I don’t know where I’m going,” he sings on Bleed, as strings gently rise and fall around him, “but it feels like I’ve been here before”: a neat capturing of a very mid-50s kind of malaise. An affecting sense of weariness seeps into everything, even the ostensibly optimistic – and utterly lovely – closer Beyond the Light comes filled with evocations of lost “nameless days” and of “the dying of the light”.

Unfortunately for Beck, Ride Lonesome does little to dispel the aforementioned theory about his best work being born out of unhappiness. There’ll be consolation in the fact it’s also that rarest of things: a sequel to a sequel that’s every bit as good as its predecessors.

Ride Lonesome is released on 18 September

The London hospital funded by donors who invested in the slave trade

The Guardian Mon, 14 Sep 2026 13:00:58 GMT

St Barts is one of many UK institutions whose benefactors were involved in the trafficking of enslaved Africans

Inside the Great Hall of St Bartholomew’s North Wing, alongside stately portraits of the apostle from whom London’s oldest hospital takes its name and King Henry VIII, extravagant commemorative boards adorn the walls.

The Great Hall was a grand, formal space where governors weighed their philanthropic donations and drafted their wills, many while investing in the stock of companies built on the trafficking of enslaved Africans. Today, many of those donors are commemorated in acrylic gold paint on the boards.

The Register of British Slave Traders, a joint venture between Lancaster University, the University of Manchester and University College London, includes biographical data on every known investor in Britain’s transatlantic trafficking of enslaved African people from the 16th to 19th centuries.

It reveals how wealthy individuals, often enriched by the proceeds from racialised chattel enslavement, donated to hundreds of church parishes and helped to fund schools, hospitals and charities across the country.

Prof William Pettigrew, who led the project, said the register had established connections with roughly 900 organisations. “Most of those organisations sought to improve the lives of ordinary Britons,” he added.

The register reveals at least 50 people with deep financial ties to St Barts who are directly linked to this history.

Among the names etched on to the boards in the Great Hall is Sir Jeffrey Jeffreys, a London merchant who left an unspecified sum to the hospital in his will. In 1694, the Jeffreys-funded ship Hannibal, commanded by Capt Thomas Phillips, docked in Barbados. This concluded a harrowing journey in which only 372 of the 700 enslaved African people bought at Whydah (Ouidah in modern-day Benin) survived the Atlantic crossing.

The grand Hogarth Stair, which leads to the Great Hall, adorned with paintings depicting healing. Photograph: Wayne Crichlow/The Guardian

The grand Hogarth Stair, which leads to the Great Hall, adorned with paintings depicting healing. Photograph: Wayne Crichlow/The Guardian

Keep scrolling

Phillips’s journal, one of the few surviving records of the voyage, details the horrors onboard, where captives were subjected to branding and calculated psychological cruelty. “Then we marked the slaves we had bought in the breast or shoulder, with a hot iron, having the letter of the ship’s name on it,” he wrote. The Africans on his ship, he recorded, held “a more dreadful apprehension of Barbadoes than we have of hell”.

Phillips recalled using African overseers, who were enslaved themselves, to keep order, whipping any plotters of mutiny. There were grave consequences of the squalid conditions on the ship; many who died on the Hannibal were killed by smallpox, dysentery, starvation and suicide. Some were thrown overboard when dead or dying to prevent the spread of disease and to protect profits.

The voyage’s mortality rate was close to 50%, cementing its place as one of the deadliest crossings in the history of the transatlantic trafficking of enslaved Africans.

The 1694 Hannibal crossing was one of 13 to which Jeffreys was financially linked. The London merchant was a director of the Royal African Company from 1684-86, and from 1692-98. His latter term coincided with the end of the company’s royal monopoly on trading enslaved Africans, from which he profited handsomely. He also inherited a fortune from his tobacco-trading uncle, John Jeffreys, in 1688. During Jeffrey Jeffreys’ time with the RAC, the organisation made 170 crossings.

Others commemorated at St Barts have links to the trafficking of enslaved Africans. Edward Colston, whose statue was toppled by Black Lives Matter protesters in Bristol in June 2020, appears in the register. William Prichard, once president of St Barts and a leading City merchant, bought £600 of RAC stock in January 1678.

Sir Robert Geffrye, who left money to the hospital and other philanthropic causes in his will, was a substantial investor in the trafficking of enslaved Africans, selling £1,600 (the equivalent of £350,000 today) of RAC stock on 5 January 1692 alone. Diane Abbott, the MP for Hackney North and Stoke Newington, has called for the removal of Geffrye’s statue at the Museum of the Home in Hoxton.

These connections run through the heart of the City of London’s political structure, with several lord mayors commemorated in the Great Hall. Sir William Humphreys, who left legacies to three London hospitals including St Barts, sat on the RAC’s court of assistants from 1683-85 and from 1688-90. In 1711, he attended Board of Trade hearings on the company’s operations on the west African coast, three years before he became lord mayor.

His predecessor, Samuel Stanier, who also left money to St Barts in his will, sold off most of his substantial £4,000 holding in the RAC in February 1698, before his lord mayoralty started in 1713.

After the British crown was restored in 1660, the trafficking of enslaved Africans became more formalised and was a lucrative source of funds for merchants.

Several leading City merchants who invested in companies linked to the enslavement of African people are commemorated in the Great Hall at St Barts. Photograph: Wayne Crichlow/The Guardian

Several leading City merchants who invested in companies linked to the enslavement of African people are commemorated in the Great Hall at St Barts. Photograph: Wayne Crichlow/The Guardian

Keep scrolling

The private banker Sir Robert Vyner (also known as Viner) became a central figure in the City and was lord mayor of London from 1674-75. He first invested in the Company of Royal Adventurers in January 1663; by August, his holding had grown to two shares, worth £800. In January 1665, he bought a further £1,200 from the Countess of Chesterfield, and was elected to the company’s board where he served from 1667-70.

He continued attending board meetings, without formally serving, from 1671 until the company’s dissolution. This positioned him to invest heavily in the RAC, the Adventurers’ successor, subscribing with £5,000 (the equivalent of £1.18m today) and serving as an assistant from 1672-74. During his involvement with both companies, they undertook 81 crossings. Vyner left a portion of the remainder of his estate to St Barts after his death in 1688.

Like St Thomas’ hospital in Lambeth, south London, St Barts provided free medical care to the city’s sick and poor people, sustained by charitable donations from City merchants and rental income from land and property across the capital.

Last year, the stairwell leading to the Great Hall was restored and rehung with William Hogarth’s The Good Samaritan and The Pool of Bethesda. The hall’s baroque ceiling carries its own coded message, its botanical motifs – oak leaves for strength, laurel wreaths for triumph and palm branches for peace – all tied to themes of healthcare.

St Barts has acknowledged its links to slavery: Barts health NHS trust archives produced an official research guide in 2024 setting out the known history and how to investigate it further, though the trust has not commissioned a stand-alone enslavement report.

A spokesperson for the trust said it was “well aware that some notable individuals historically associated with our hospitals profited from the transatlantic slave trade”, and they were identified in the Great Hall because of their donations.

“As further information comes to light we are discussing with Barts Charity and Barts Heritage, which manages the listed building, how we could most appropriately acknowledge the full story behind these historic links.”

A spokesperson for Barts Charity, which supports the trust, said that, previously, “detailed research has not established whether, or to what extent, particular gifts can be traced into the assets managed by the charity today. We are reviewing the new findings with Barts Health and Barts Heritage and considering any appropriate next steps.”

In 2023, the Scott Trust, the Guardian’s sole owner, published research showing the founder of the Manchester Guardian and his backers profited from the enslavement of African people in Jamaica and the US. In response, the Scott Trust launched the Cotton Capital series and the Legacies of Enslavement programme, a ten-year restorative justice initiative.

Andy Burnham cancels engagements as his father’s death is announced

Andy Burnham has cancelled his engagements for Monday and Tuesday after his father, Roy, died.

Burnham’s father had Alzheimer’s and was in a care home. In an interview Burnham gave in July, he said his father’s condition meant he was unaware that his son was about to become prime minister.

“That’s a sadness because he would be [proud],” Burnham told the Times. “But the way I look at it, it’s his achievement as well. A whole family achievement, although he doesn’t know it.”

Burnham has talked about wanting to improve social care, in part because of his experiences with his father.

In one of his first speeches as prime minister, Burnham said it was humbling to see the “skill and the care and the professionalism” of care workers like those looking after his father, and that they should be paid more.

Among those expressing their condolences was Angela Rayner, the housing secretary, who posted: “My thoughts are with Andy and his family at this terribly difficult and sad time.”

In her own post on X, Kemi Badenoch, the Conservative leader, offered her condolences to Burnham and his family, adding: “No matter how old you are, or how much you try to prepare, losing your father is a profoundly painful experience.

“A part of your life that has always been there is suddenly gone forever and it can feel as though a part of you won’t ever be the same again.”

At the start of the Commons session on Monday afternoon, Lindsay Hoyle, the speaker, said: “I am sure the whole house will want to send our best wishes to him and his family at this sad time.”

In Head North, the 2024 book he co-wrote with Steve Rotheram, the Liverpool city region mayor, Burnham described what he said had been a happy upbringing with his father, his mother, Eileen, and his two brothers in Culcheth, near Warrington in Cheshire. Roy worked as a telephone engineer, while Eileen was a GP’s receptionist.

“Neither my dad, Roy, nor my mum, Eileen, went to university. But both could have done if they had grown up in a different time and in a different place,” he wrote.

“Their knowledge of that fact seemed to make them all the more determined that their three sons would go. But that did not make them pushy parents in any way.

“Their approach was one of quiet encouragement and confidence-building. Our family home in Culcheth was always full of music, life, laughter, love and support.”

There’s a surprisingly simple reason for England’s high antidepressant use: lots of people need them

The Guardian Mon, 14 Sep 2026 12:00:58 GMT

The idea that GPs are ignoring guidelines and ‘overprescribing’ doesn’t hold water. Instead, look to our social and economic crises

Dean Burnett is a doctor of neuroscience

A new NHS report has revealed the highest ever levels of antidepressant use recorded in England, with roughly one in seven people prescribed an antidepressant item in 2025-26. This has resulted in a swathe of media coverage expressing alarm over the increase, with questions about what could, or should, be done to reverse the trend.

Such a high level of antidepressant use should, of course, prompt concern and reflection. But the popular claim that has taken hold is that antidepressant use is too high because of “overprescribing”, as Dr John Read, a professor of clinical psychology, says in the Daily Mail. This is the idea that patients are being prescribed antidepressants when they shouldn’t be, or when better, safer alternatives are available.

This idea is worth challenging – but first it’s important to consider how we got here. The increase in antidepressant use is strongly correlated with a rise in diagnoses in common disorders including depression and anxiety. Much of this is the afterlife of the Covid-19 pandemic and its associated lockdowns: according to ONS data, across Britain, the rate of depressive symptoms in adults doubled during the crisis to almost one in five. As of April 2025, the figures remain almost as high. This surge has particularly affected young people in England, with one in four having a mental health condition, according to NHS data.

So with this rise, an increase in antidepressant use is predictable. Lockdown, however necessary for public health, has had lasting implications for the country’s wellbeing.

But it’s not only the consequences of the pandemic. What this data also indicates is that persistent regional inequalities have a worsening effect on mental health outcomes, and therefore antidepressant use. The most dramatic increases in antidepressant use are found in the most impoverished regions of England, while more affluent regions report modest levels of antidepressant use.

The highest rate of antidepressant use was seen in patients treated under the North East and North Cumbria integrated care board, with 200 in every 1,000 people prescribed antidepressant medication. Consider that this ICB contains some of the country’s most deprived areas, which have “faced longstanding inequalities and poor health for decades”, and you have further proof of something that has long been clear: poverty is inextricably linked to poorer mental health outcomes. One key element that underpins many cases of depression, anxiety and related disorders is chronic stress. It’s our brain’s achilles heel. And a guaranteed source of chronic stress is a life of constant poverty.

The argument presented against wide antidepressant prescription, as laid out in the Daily Mail, is that “doctors [are] increasingly being expected to treat wider social and life problems with medication”. Such a position assumes that a neat division can be drawn between these social problems and the mental health conditions they produce.

These socioeconomic factors also explain why antidepressants are used more and more as a first-line treatment. It’s all well and good to argue that less severe cases of depression should be treated with talking therapies such as cognitive behavioural therapy, but these involve regular one-one-one sessions with trained counsellors, and the wait for such interventions on the NHS regularly lasts months, if not years.

In the most deprived areas, access to such services is even more difficult, whereas for the most part, antidepressants are accessible straight away. It should also be said that GPs follow strict clinical guidelines for prescribing antidepressants, as set out by the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence. These state that practitioners should “not routinely offer antidepressant medication as first-line treatment for less severe depression unless that is the person’s preference”. So it is clear that GPs are not simply handing out pills, but rather responding to legitimate patient demand.

Of course, antidepressants can’t be a magic bullet – mental health services are evidently in need of deep reform and increased funding. We have already heard pledges to improve services, including with the government’s announcement in May this year of a new mental health strategy in England to drive a shift from crisis intervention to preventive care. And there are already technological interventions being recommended, including digital therapies for depression and anxiety that “could free up thousands of NHS therapist hours”.

after newsletter promotion

The government’s callout for frontline workers, clinicians and mental health experts to share views on transforming mental health care shows that there are likely several creative solutions to tackle this crisis, without the need for medication. Still, there should be no doubt about the simple reality: more people than ever are taking antidepressants because they genuinely need them.

So the point here is not that the record rates of antidepressant use in England isn’t a problem. It undoubtedly is. But to determine that this is due to “overprescription” is to mistake a symptom for a much deeper social and economic crisis as its cause.

Dean Burnett is a doctor of neuroscience and the author of The Idiot Brain and Emotional Ignorance

Touring can take musicians to isolating, anxious extremes. Access to therapy on the road is a vital support

The Guardian Mon, 14 Sep 2026 12:00:58 GMT

I know from our early days how high-pressure road life can be. While big tours often hire therapists, grassroots acts can’t afford it. I’m pleased to back a new scheme that aims to change that

When Radiohead started touring, it was hugely exciting, but we got signed when we had been going for five or six years and had only really played in Oxford. Suddenly you’re entering a new world: the first flush of fame, being compared to everyone else, the furnace-like experience when a band takes off and a whole new routine of late nights, bad food and everything else that goes on around live music. Everything is heightened and it can be very isolating.

In 1992 we were playing small venues in a van and then suddenly in 1993 we were spending the second half of the year in the US. On our second long tour that year, everything caught up with me. I kind of withdrew into myself. Something about being in the US made me feel “impostor syndrome”. I really did feel a very long way from home. All that anxiety has to come out somewhere – for some it’s drink and drugs – but for me it came out in my playing. There was one particular show where we were opening for Tears for Fears and another band who had [Blondie’s] Clem Burke on drums. Clem was my absolute drummer hero but I just hit peak overwhelm, and my drumming went off a cliff. Every limb seemed to be going at its own speed. The kick drum became like trying to open a heavy door.

By the end of the tour it was very noticeable. I was lucky in that I could speak to my wife – this was pre-Zoom or FaceTime, so meant very expensive phone calls! – but after that tour one of our managers asked me to go and have a chat and broached it with me very nicely. Having that space to begin talking about it was absolutely invaluable. Similarly, when we opened for James and then REM, they became kind of mentors: seeing how other people navigate it all was fascinating.

On Radiohead’s tour last autumn, with the help of the Music Industry Therapist Collective, we were able to put an initiative in place to support the health and well-being of all tour personnel. The MITC provided introductory sessions during rehearsals and production build, and confidential drop-in therapy sessions were available to anyone in the touring party during the tour if they wanted them. But until now there’s been nothing like that available for bands playing venues like the ones we did when we started.

At that level, your margins are nonexistent, your workload is much greater – loading the gear and so on – and you’re driving yourself between shows. You’re expected to get your head down and get on with it, but it can mean times when you’re not necessarily looking after yourself physically and you can feel very isolated. There’s an emotional and geographical displacement in moving from place to place and living on top of each other. There’s the sound check, the gig, meeting people afterwards, anxiety that some people guiding you may not have your best interests at heart. You can feel really vulnerable, and there’s no way of getting off that roundabout until you get home. It’s difficult to talk about because nobody wants to rock the boat, and other people might be going through the same thing, so you don’t want to burden them.

That’s why I’m supporting a new project called the Pay It Forward Fund, which has been set up by Tamsin Embleton and the Music Industry Therapist Collective to provide much-needed mental health support for musicians and crews on smaller tours, having grown out of the kind of help MITC already provides to larger tours. If someone is looking to reach out to a therapist, it can be really good to talk to someone who has lived experience in the music industry, so this project will mean people have someone to talk to who understands what they’re going through. I’ve volunteered for the Samaritans since I was a student and know how important it is to talk.

I’d have really appreciated something like the Pay It Forward Fund back in Radiohead’s early days, so that’s the kind of space I hope it can provide. Initially £272,000 is being provided to finance 150 tour teams of practitioners over a three-year period, an occupational health, mental health education and pastoral care programme for crews and artists on smaller tours. Hopefully after that it will become an everyday part of touring and make the sort of difference it would have done for me. You might be on the other side of the world, but you can reach out and talk to somebody face to face.

Applications for the Pay It Forward Fund are now open. MITC’s book Touring and Mental Health: the Music Industry Manual, edited by Tamsin Embleton, is published by Omnibus

Islamophobia is rising – and Britain’s politicians have been dangerously complacent in tackling it

The Guardian Mon, 14 Sep 2026 11:00:56 GMT

Mainstream figures have been enabling anti-Muslim racism, creating the ideal conditions for the rise of hard-right political parties

Five years ago, many Muslims wondered if the prejudices they faced were set to fade away. The “war on terror” was dwindling in prominence, and new enemies such as Russia seemed to be displacing fears of Islamic terrorism. Yet Britain’s Islamophobia has only intensified since then. A poll published in July found that two out of five Britons believe Muslims cannot integrate into British society. Earlier in the summer, it was reported that more than half of Muslims in Britain had personally experienced anti-Islam prejudice in the last year, and a quarter in a public place.

The evidence of a worsening climate for Muslims has been mounting since two summers ago, when racist riots erupted across the UK, targeting mosques and asylum hostels. Watching videos of those events, I was disturbed by the parents who brought their young children to watch while mobs attempted, with apparently murderous intent, to break into the buildings. It was not only hardened far-right activists but a much broader cross-section of British society that was willing to participate in racist violence directed at Muslims or asylum seekers assumed to be Muslim.

But it is the widespread indifference to anti-Muslim racist violence that is most distressing. Last October, a white man raped a Sikh woman in her Walsall home while shouting Islamophobic abuse, believing her to be Muslim, and telling her he was a “British master”. The case attracted little public comment, despite seeming to be part of a pattern of racist sexual crimes in the region. Likewise, there was only modest coverage of the rampaging knife attack that began at an Edinburgh mosque in June that left a number of men injured.

To understand why Islamophobia is so pervasive, we need to grasp the deeper forces that enable it. The first is a bedrock of anti-Islam attitudes set during the 1990s when, with the cold war over, neoconservative intellectuals began to see in Islam a new enemy to replace communism. After Muslim protests against Salman Rushdie’s The Satanic Verses, some liberal commentators also began to declare that Islam was incompatible with western values. That all might have remained a problem of cultural adaptation to be solved through community-building, but during the “war on terror”, anti-Muslim racism was institutionalised in the daily functioning of the British state by the Labour government. Ministers made regular speeches singling out Muslim communities as threats, while under the Prevent policy, thousands of public sector workers were trained to regard ordinary Muslim political and religious behaviours as indicators of extremism.

The second has to do with Palestine. The groundswell of opposition to Israel’s genocide in Gaza has been profoundly disconcerting to Britain’s foreign policy establishment. In turn, the hundreds of thousands of people who marched on demonstrations have been depicted as supporters of, or aligned with, Islamic extremism. That has restored a virulent atmosphere of animosity towards Muslims, who are again seen as dangerous and disloyal.

We might think, for example, of Keir Starmer’s description of planned protests on 7 October 2025 as “un-British”, his suggestion that further protests could be banned and his call for prosecution against demonstrators using contested phrases such as “globalise the intifada” – despite repeated explanations that such slogans are not calls for violence. His comments reflect a widespread belief that ordinary protest – against a genocide! – is actually something else: the importing by Muslims and their allies of dangerous foreign ideologies. But to say that is to demonise the bond of allegiance between Muslims in the west and Muslims in other parts of the world fighting colonial occupations. That community-based international solidarity, of the kind that Britain used to hold up as evidence of its tolerance, should only be welcomed.

Third, there are the barriers that make it hard to even raise the issue of anti-Muslim racism in a fruitful way. Talk about Islamophobia in the mainstream of British public life and you will face the ritual demand that you also condemn Islamic extremism and acknowledge antisemitism among Muslims. Of course, an attack on a synagogue is to be condemned as forcefully as an attack on a mosque. But the harder political question is how to create the conditions in which neither one of those attacks is made likely. In this, Jewish communities have the resolute support of the British government. Muslims do not. For decades, they have been on the receiving end of official disdain, and when they attempt to assert a modicum of political representation they are accused of “family voting”.

This matters because racism is about power. Its function is to divide society so that certain groups can be subjected to exceptional forms of exploitation or elimination. It is typically experienced as routine and structured powerlessness: the daily struggle to eke out a living in the face of discriminatory employers, public services riddled with suspicion, oppressive policing, immigration enforcement. Twenty-five years ago, policymakers at least paid lip service to racism as “institutional”, which helped to make visible some of its structural features. But that is no longer true. Racism is nowadays framed mainly as a problem of extremist individuals radicalised by hateful and polarising ideologies.

Tackling racism means overcoming that lack of power. But the opposite is happening as governing elites continuously reinforce racist attitudes. A decision, for instance, to allow Ukrainians fleeing war preferential entry to the UK while many Afghans fleeing war have to risk their lives in dangerous sea crossings – a policy of racial segregation that is as absolute and violent as those of the Jim Crow south of the US – is also a form of public messaging. Policymakers can hardly be surprised when ordinary people take their cue from such policies and decide that non-white immigrants must indeed be a threat to national identity. Racism applied at the border inevitably seeps into other areas of public life.

Then there is the other response to talking about Islamophobia: to switch the conversation to a victimhood competition, the never-ending game of fighting over whose oppression is greater, as if there were some way to rank Black people, Jews and Muslims by the scale of horrors they have experienced. What this misses is that the fate of Muslims is inseparable from the fate of all people of colour in the UK. What Britain does to Muslims today it is likely to do to Black people tomorrow, and vice versa. And if a future government of Britain decided to carry out the mass deportation of Muslims from the country, I have no doubt it would decide soon afterwards to do the same to Jews. When supporters of Israel promote Islamophobia, they are playing with fascist fires that will end up engulfing us all.

after newsletter promotion

For decades, Britain’s mainstream political leaders have been enabling anti-Muslim racism, creating the ideal conditions for the rise of hard-right political parties. They continue to do so, sleepwalking to social disaster with an unconscionable recklessness and complacency. It is high time they woke up.

Arun Kundnani is editorial director of Monthly Review Press

Spanish GP plans to change Madring after fierce criticism from F1 drivers

The Guardian Mon, 14 Sep 2026 10:57:28 GMT

New track for Spanish GP frustrated drivers and fans

McLaren’s Stella: ‘It’s impossible to attempt overtaking’

Discussions are already under way to change the layout of Formula One’s newest circuit after driver condemnation of the Madring during its inaugural grand prix. The race in Madrid was won by Mercedes’ Kimi Antonelli, but it was notable for being a procession with overtakes failing to reach double digits over 57 laps. Drivers were left frustrated and disappointed at an opportunity that had been lost, resulting in a chorus of criticism.

“I don’t know how someone looks at this design and goes ‘mint’,” said the defending world champion, Lando Norris, who finished third. “There’s a lot of opportunity. They can make it into a track that’s good for racing and I’m excited to come back here next year if they can make these changes.

“The fact you have to turn and brake basically defeats the whole object of racing. They can do some simple changes. I hope they do it because then it should be more exciting for everyone.”

The race was far from thrilling with drivers largely circulating behind one another, albeit at high speed, but unable to find any opportunity to make a move. Audi’s Gabriel Bortoleto dismissively categorised it as uninvigorating to drive in as it had been to watch. “I almost fell asleep as well,” he said.

The Madring, a hybrid circuit of part public roads and part purpose-built track, has been constructed in north-east Madrid around a conference centre on the way to the airport. Logistically, it has been a success, with transport to and from the track managed well, despite the huge numbers of fans, which F1 puts at 352,000 for the weekend.

The teams enjoyed the facilities and space and it presented a high-speed and spectacular challenge on a narrow, technical circuit many drivers enjoyed over a single lap in qualifying. However, in racing terms, the track, built at a reported cost of approximately £71m, was frustrating.

It was designed by the Italian Jarno Zaffelli who said he hoped “people walk away recognising it’s possible to build a street circuit that is not boring”. That was a goal left sorely wanting after the race, with people walking away looking bored.

“There are some corners that need to be changed to create more overtaking opportunities because it’s nice over one lap, but in the race you’re just stuck behind,” said Antonelli.

His feelings were echoed by Max Verstappen who finished second. “If you just drive a little bit in the middle, then you can’t pass,” he said. Verstappen had warned of the poor design from the moment he had first driven the track in a simulator.

The Mercedes team principal, Toto Wolff, acknowledged there were discussions about changes taking place even before the race. “The tricky bit [is] doing a track that is spectacular for the drivers and then building it in a way that there is lots of overtaking,” he said. “I had a discussion [on Saturday] with the CEO of the circuit and they are totally open-minded about next year.
